practice_questions.text:
Which of the following metals is classified as ferrous?
A) Aluminium
B) Copper
C) Mild steel
D) Zinc
practice_questions.marks: C) Mild steel [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two physical properties of metals that a designer would consider when selecting a material for electrical wiring.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: electrical conductivity / thermal conductivity / density / melting point. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between malleability and ductility.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Malleability is the ability of a metal to be shaped by compressive forces such as hammering or rolling without cracking.
• Ductility is the ability of a metal to be drawn out into a wire by a tensile (pulling) force without breaking.
• A metal can be malleable without being highly ductile; for example, lead is very malleable but only moderately ductile, whereas copper is both highly malleable and highly ductile. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why aluminium is preferred over mild steel for the manufacture of aircraft body panels.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Aluminium has a much lower density (approx. 2.7 g/cm³) compared to mild steel (approx. 7.85 g/cm³), significantly reducing the overall mass of the aircraft.
• A lower mass reduces fuel consumption and increases payload capacity, both of which are critical for commercial aircraft operation.
• Aluminium forms a natural oxide layer that provides good corrosion resistance without additional coatings, reducing maintenance costs.
• Despite its lower density, aluminium alloys (e.g. duralumin) can achieve sufficient tensile strength for structural applications.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the ecological and social impacts of extracting metals from the Earth’s crust, and discuss how designers can reduce these impacts in their material choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Ecological impacts: open-cast mining removes topsoil and destroys habitats; tailings and leachate pollute waterways with heavy metals; smelting releases CO₂ and SO₂, contributing to climate change and acid rain.
Social impacts: mining communities in lower-income countries may face poor working conditions, health hazards from dust and toxic chemicals, and community displacement.
Designer responses: specifying recycled metals where possible (recycled aluminium uses only 5% of the energy of virgin smelting); choosing metals from certified ethical supply chains; designing for disassembly so metals can be recovered at end of life; minimising material waste through efficient cutting plans.
[6 marks — Mastering: Balanced, developed coverage of both ecological and social impacts plus at least two specific designer responses linked to named metals. Secure: Two impacts and one designer response with some development. Developing: One impact and one response, limited development. Emerging: Vague reference to environmental harm without specific examples.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using stainless steel compared with mild steel for the manufacture of kitchen cutlery.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of stainless steel:
• Contains at least 10.5% chromium, which forms a self-repairing oxide layer, making it highly resistant to corrosion from food acids and washing.
• Hygienic surface that does not react with food; important for food safety.
• Aesthetically appealing; retains a polished appearance over many years without surface treatments.
• Hard and maintains a sharp edge on knives.
Disadvantages of stainless steel:
• Significantly more expensive than mild steel due to the alloying elements (chromium, nickel) and more complex refining.
• More difficult to machine and form than mild steel; harder on tooling, increasing manufacturing cost.
• Poorer thermal conductivity than mild steel (relevant if cutlery is heated, though less critical than for cookware).
• Mild steel is cheaper to purchase, easier to machine and weld, but would require plating or coating to prevent rust, adding cost and potential delamination issues.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion, at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with reference to specific properties and manufacturing considerations. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or superficial response.]

practice_questions.text:
Which component would be most suitable as the input device in an automatic security light that switches on at dusk?
A) Buzzer
B) LED
C) Light-dependent resistor
D) Motor
practice_questions.marks: C) Light-dependent resistor [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the three stages of the input-process-output model.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any two correctly named stages; 2 marks for all three: input, process, output. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a thermistor is used as part of an electronic control system for a greenhouse heater.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• The thermistor is connected in the input stage of the circuit and its resistance changes with temperature.
• When the greenhouse temperature falls, the thermistor's resistance increases, raising the voltage at the processor's input.
• The processor detects this change and switches on the heater (output device) to warm the greenhouse. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a moisture sensor detects when a plant pot needs watering and communicates this to the rest of the system.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The moisture sensor has two conductive tracks separated by a small gap in the soil.
• When the soil is dry, there is no electrical path between the tracks and no current flows to the processor.
• When the soil is moist, water bridges the gap, completing the circuit and allowing current to flow.
• The processor detects this current change and triggers an output device (e.g. LED indicator or buzzer) to alert the user.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a closed-loop and an open-loop electronic control system. Use an example of each in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• An open-loop system has no feedback — the output runs for a fixed time or at a fixed level regardless of the result. Example: a timer-controlled toaster runs for a set period whether or not the bread is toasted.
• A closed-loop system continuously monitors the output and feeds this information back to the processor to adjust the system's behaviour. Example: a central heating thermostat uses a thermistor to measure room temperature and cuts off the boiler when the target temperature is reached.
• Open-loop systems are simpler and cheaper to manufacture; closed-loop systems are more precise and suitable for safety-critical applications.
[6 marks — Mastering: Both types explained with accurate examples and a developed comparison of advantages. Secure: Both types named and explained with examples but comparison limited. Developing: One type explained clearly; second type superficial. Emerging: Partial or confused identification of one type.]

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating an automatic door opener for a supermarket entrance. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using an electronic sensor-based system rather than a manual push-button to control the door.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
• A sensor-based system (e.g. infrared motion sensor) responds automatically without the user touching anything, improving accessibility for wheelchair users and those carrying bags.
• The system can be programmed to detect multiple inputs simultaneously (e.g. door position sensor + motion sensor) for greater safety.
• Automatic systems reduce wear on manual hardware over time and can be updated by reprogramming without physical changes.
Disadvantages:
• Electronic systems are more expensive to design, install and maintain than a simple push-button.
• Sensor malfunctions (e.g. false triggers from sunlight or small animals) can cause doors to open inappropriately, creating security or energy-efficiency issues.
• Power dependency means the door fails to open during power cuts unless a battery backup is fitted, which adds further cost.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages, including context of the supermarket entrance. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages identified with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided response or very superficial points.]

practice_questions.text:
Which type of board is made from a fluted inner layer sandwiched between two flat liner sheets?
A) Solid white board
B) Duplex board
C) Corrugated card
D) Mount board
practice_questions.marks: C) Corrugated card [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two papers suitable for use in the initial design development stages of a graphics project.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: layout paper / tracing paper / cartridge paper / bleed-proof paper / grid paper. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how paper is manufactured from wood pulp.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
- Wood is chipped and treated to separate cellulose fibres into a pulp slurry.
- The slurry is spread onto a moving wire mesh where water drains away and fibres mat together.
- The web passes through press rollers and heated drying cylinders to remove remaining moisture and form a continuous roll. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why grain direction is important when cutting and folding a net for a cardboard carton.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- During manufacture, paper fibres align in the machine direction (grain direction).
- Paper and board are harder to fold across the grain, so aligning the grain along the fold lines reduces the force needed to score and crease.
- Folding against the grain can crack the surface coating and weaken the structure of the carton.
- Specifying grain direction correctly during print finishing reduces waste and improves the quality of the assembled box. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a packaging designer might choose duplex board rather than solid white board for a breakfast cereal box, considering both performance and sustainability.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Duplex board has a white bleached top surface suitable for high-quality printing, meeting the visual requirements of cereal-box branding.
- The grey recycled-fibre back layer reduces raw material cost compared with solid white board, which uses 100% virgin chemical pulp.
- Using recycled fibre in the core layers reduces energy consumption and water use during manufacture, lowering the carbon footprint of the packaging.
- Solid white board offers superior whiteness and colour accuracy, which may be justified for premium products where brand colour precision is critical.
- For a budget cereal brand, the cost saving of duplex board outweighs the marginal loss in print quality; for a luxury brand, solid white board may be justified.
[6 marks - Mastering: Balanced comparison referencing both material performance and sustainability with application to the cereal box context. Secure: Performance and sustainability points made but comparison lacks full development. Developing: One board described well; limited comparison. Emerging: Basic identification only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using recycled fibre rather than virgin wood pulp in the manufacture of paper and board products.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
- Recycled fibre uses significantly less energy and water than processing virgin wood pulp, reducing the environmental impact of manufacture.
- Using recycled content diverts waste paper and board from landfill, extending the useful life of the raw material.
- Recycled-content products can carry on-pack environmental claims that appeal to environmentally conscious consumers and retail buyers.
- Reduces demand for virgin timber, helping to protect forests and the biodiversity they support.
Disadvantages:
- Each recycling cycle shortens the cellulose fibres, reducing tensile strength and making it harder to produce high-quality printing surfaces.
- Recycled board is typically grey or brown in colour; achieving a white surface requires a virgin-fibre top ply, adding cost and complexity.
- Ink contamination in recycled streams must be removed by de-inking, which adds a processing stage and produces sludge waste requiring disposal.
- The quality and availability of recycled fibre fluctuates with consumer recycling rates, making supply chains less predictable than virgin pulp sourcing.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages, linked to real design or manufacturing contexts. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages identified with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance between sides. Emerging: One-sided response or very superficial points.]

practice_questions.text:
Which fibre is produced by extruding a liquid polymer through spinnerets?
A) Cotton
B) Linen
C) Polyester
D) Wool
practice_questions.marks: C) Polyester [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two natural animal fibres used in textile production.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: wool, silk, cashmere, alpaca. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe three properties of cotton that make it suitable for T-shirts.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Cotton is soft and comfortable against the skin.
• It is highly absorbent, drawing perspiration away from the body.
• It is breathable, allowing air to circulate and helping to regulate body temperature. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why polycotton (65% polyester / 35% cotton) is used for school shirts rather than 100% cotton.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The polyester content makes the fabric more durable and resistant to wear, extending the garment's life.
• Polyester dries quickly after washing and resists creasing, reducing ironing time for parents.
• The cotton content retains breathability and softness, keeping the shirt comfortable to wear all day.
• Blending reduces material cost compared to 100% cotton, making the garment more affordable.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the environmental concerns associated with the production of synthetic fibres and evaluate one strategy manufacturers use to reduce this impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Synthetic fibres such as polyester and nylon are derived from crude oil, a finite non-renewable resource, so their production depletes fossil fuel reserves.
• Manufacturing processes are energy-intensive and release greenhouse gases, contributing to climate change.
• Each wash of a synthetic garment releases hundreds of thousands of microplastic fibres that enter waterways and the food chain, harming aquatic ecosystems.
• Strategy: recycled polyester (rPET) is made by reprocessing plastic bottles or post-consumer textile waste, using approximately 59% less energy than virgin polyester.
• Limitation: rPET still sheds microplastics, and sorting mixed-fibre garments for recycling remains technically difficult, so impact is reduced but not eliminated.
[6 marks — Mastering: Two environmental concerns explained fully plus strategy evaluated with limitation. Secure: Two concerns and strategy named but limited evaluation. Developing: One concern explained; strategy mentioned superficially. Emerging: Partial or vague points.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using natural fibres compared with synthetic fibres for a sportswear manufacturer designing performance running kit.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of natural fibres for running kit:
• Merino wool is naturally moisture-wicking and odour-resistant (wool fibre structure absorbs vapour but wicks liquid), reducing unpleasant smells during extended runs.
• Natural fibres are generally more biodegradable at end of life, reducing landfill impact.
Disadvantages of natural fibres for running kit:
• Wool and cotton are heavier than synthetic equivalents when dry, and significantly heavier when wet, affecting performance.
• Natural fibres are typically more expensive and can take longer to dry than synthetics such as polyester.
Advantages of synthetics for running kit:
• Polyester is lightweight, durable and quick-drying; adding elastane provides stretch and close fit without restricting movement.
• Synthetics can be engineered to specific performance specifications (e.g. reflective yarns, UV protection) that natural fibres cannot match.
Disadvantages of synthetics for running kit:
• Synthetics absorb little moisture and can feel clammy; they also retain odour-causing bacteria more readily than natural fibres.
• Microplastic shedding from synthetic sportswear during washing is an environmental harm that many consumers now consider.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion, at least two developed points per side linked specifically to running kit context. Secure: Points identified with some development, reasonable balance. Developing: Listed points, limited development, imbalanced. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial.]

practice_questions.text:
Which manufactured board is produced by bonding wood veneers with alternating grain directions?
A) MDF
B) Chipboard
C) Plywood
D) Hardboard
practice_questions.marks: C) Plywood [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two softwood species used in the manufacture of timber products.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: Scots pine / spruce / larch / western red cedar (or other recognised softwood species). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how kiln seasoning reduces the moisture content of timber.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Converted timber is placed inside a heated chamber where temperature, humidity and airflow are precisely controlled.
• Heat causes the moisture inside the timber to evaporate and be drawn out through the controlled airflow.
• The process can reduce timber to any required moisture content within days or weeks, far faster than air seasoning. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why MDF is chosen over solid timber for a painted kitchen cabinet door panel.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• MDF has a perfectly smooth, knot-free surface because it is made from fine fibres compressed under heat and pressure, so paint adheres evenly without grain showing through.
• MDF is dimensionally stable and will not warp or move with humidity changes as much as solid timber, keeping the door panel flat.
• MDF is available in large, consistent sheets so a cabinet door can be cut without waste from natural defects such as knots.
• It can be machined with a router to produce clean, precise profiles on the edge of the door panel.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the environmental and ethical considerations a designer should take into account when selecting mahogany for a range of premium furniture. Use specific examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Mahogany is a slow-growing tropical hardwood; over-harvesting has caused significant deforestation of tropical rainforests, destroying biodiversity and releasing stored carbon.
• Specifying FSC-certified mahogany ensures the timber comes from a forest managed sustainably with replanting and ecosystem protection.
• Reclaimed mahogany salvaged from demolished buildings or old furniture offers identical properties without new felling.
• A designer could consider using a sustainable alternative with similar visual qualities, such as teak from plantation-grown sources, reducing pressure on wild mahogany populations.
• Supply chains for tropical hardwoods can involve poor labour conditions; FSC certification addresses both environmental and social standards.
[6 marks — Mastering: Two or more environmental considerations developed with specific examples and practical alternatives proposed. Secure: Environmental and ethical issues identified with some development. Developing: One area covered or points listed without development. Emerging: Vague reference to deforestation without development.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using manufactured boards rather than solid timber in the production of flat-pack bedroom furniture.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
• Manufactured boards such as chipboard and MDF are available in large, consistent sheet sizes, allowing components to be efficiently nested and CNC-cut with minimal waste.
• They are dimensionally stable; unlike solid timber, they do not shrink, swell or warp significantly with seasonal humidity changes, keeping joints tight over time.
• Sheet materials make use of lower-grade timber fibres and off-cuts, reducing the amount of high-quality solid timber needed and potentially lowering the environmental impact.
• Costs are lower than equivalent solid timber, making the finished furniture more affordable for consumers.
Disadvantages:
• Chipboard and MDF have poor edge strength; fixings such as screws pull out easily from the edge, requiring cam-lock fittings or metal inserts in flat-pack construction.
• Standard chipboard and MDF are not moisture resistant; kitchen or bathroom applications require moisture-resistant (MR) grades, which cost more.
• Manufactured boards cannot be refinished by sanding and re-varnishing in the way solid timber can, reducing the longevity of the product.
• Binders such as urea-formaldehyde in MDF and chipboard can off-gas volatile organic compounds (VOCs), a concern in enclosed bedrooms.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages, applied to flat-pack bedroom furniture context. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development or imbalanced response. Emerging: Superficial or one-sided response.]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a thermosetting polymer?
A) Acrylic (PMMA)
B) High-density polyethylene (HDPE)
C) Melamine formaldehyde
D) Polypropylene (PP)
practice_questions.marks: C) Melamine formaldehyde [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two thermoforming polymers and state one typical use for each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly named thermoforming polymer with a plausible use, up to 2 marks. Accept: acrylic — signs/light fittings; HIPS — vacuum-formed packaging/yoghurt pots; HDPE — milk bottles/cutting boards; LDPE — plastic bags; PP — food containers/bottle caps; PVC — window frames/cable insulation; PET — drinks bottles; ABS — LEGO bricks/keyboard keys. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe why thermoforming polymers can be recycled more easily than thermosetting polymers.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Thermoforming polymers have no cross-links between their polymer chains.
• Applying heat causes the chains to soften and slide past one another, allowing the material to be reshaped.
• Thermosetting polymers form permanent cross-links during curing that cannot be broken by heat, so the material cannot be remelted and recycled. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a saucepan handle is made from a thermosetting polymer rather than a thermoforming polymer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A saucepan handle must withstand high temperatures from the hob without softening or deforming.
• Thermosetting polymers such as phenol formaldehyde (Bakelite) form permanent cross-links during curing, giving them excellent heat resistance.
• A thermoforming polymer such as polypropylene would soften at the temperatures involved because its chains are not cross-linked.
• Thermosetting polymers are also good electrical insulators, providing an additional safety benefit. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the ecological and social issues associated with the widespread use of crude-oil-derived polymers in product design. Refer to specific polymer types in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Ecological: crude oil is finite and non-renewable; extraction and refining release CO₂ and pollutants; single-use polymers such as LDPE bags and PET bottles contribute to microplastic ocean pollution; thermosets cannot be recycled and end up in landfill.
Social: cheap polymers such as PVC and HDPE have enabled affordable housing improvements, medical devices and food safety; disposable packaging reduces food waste but drives linear consumption; communities near polymer production or waste sites face pollution health risks.
[6 marks — Mastering: ecological and social aspects both developed with named polymer examples and a balanced evaluation. Secure: both aspects covered, examples present but evaluation limited. Developing: one aspect developed, the other superficial. Emerging: general points about plastic pollution, no named polymers or balance.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of thermosetting polymers compared with thermoforming polymers for use in manufactured products.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of thermosets: permanent rigidity at elevated temperatures; high chemical resistance; good electrical insulation; dimensionally stable under load.
Disadvantages of thermosets: cannot be remelted or recycled; brittle compared to many thermoplastics; more difficult to manufacture (require moulds and curing cycles); limited colour range (often dark).
Advantages of thermoforming: recyclable; wide range of forming processes; diverse colours and finishes; easier to re-manufacture.
Disadvantages of thermoforming: soften at relatively low temperatures; less suitable for high-heat applications; some types degrade with UV exposure.
[8 marks — Mastering: sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed points per side, specific polymer names and product contexts used throughout. Secure: two points each side with some development and examples. Developing: points listed with limited development; unbalanced. Emerging: one-sided or very superficial with no named polymers.]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of primary research?
A) Reading a published market report
B) Watching users interact with an existing product
C) Searching a manufacturer's website
D) Looking at statistics from a government survey
practice_questions.marks: B) Watching users interact with an existing product [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two features of an effective design brief.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of two valid points from: identifies the problem to be solved; identifies the intended user or client; is open-ended (does not prescribe the solution); is concise; sets out the context clearly. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a designer could use product analysis to inform a new design for a reusable drinks bottle.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Credit: examines the materials used in existing bottles (e.g. stainless steel, BPA-free polymer) to assess suitability; tests the seal mechanism of competitor products to identify leak failure modes; measures handle diameter and bottle height against user grip data; assesses aesthetic appeal through user feedback on existing products; evaluates sustainability of existing designs (e.g. recyclability, repairability). One mark per valid, developed point. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a design brief and a design specification. Use an example product in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Design brief: a short statement identifying the problem and user without specifying the solution (1 mark) + developed explanation or example (1 mark). Design specification: a detailed list of measurable criteria the product must meet (1 mark) + developed explanation or example showing a precise, testable point (1 mark). Example: brief = 'Design a product to help hospital patients reach items on their bedside table'; design criterion: 'The reaching arm must extend to a minimum of 600 mm and support a load of 0.5 kg'. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A designer is developing a new school bag for secondary school students. Evaluate the use of a questionnaire as a primary research method for this project, discussing both advantages and disadvantages.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced, developed argument weighing advantages (reaches a large sample quickly; generates quantitative data on preferred features such as colour, strap width or number of pockets; identifies the price range users expect) against disadvantages (closed questions may miss important issues; students may give aspirational rather than honest answers; questionnaire cannot observe actual use behaviour such as how bags are loaded and carried). Concludes with a reasoned judgement on whether a questionnaire is sufficient alone or should be combined with observation. Secure: Both sides presented with some development, limited conclusion. Developing: One side only, or both sides but superficial. Emerging: Brief, undeveloped points only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: A product design company is developing a range of kitchen tools for users with limited hand strength. Write two design criteria that would be appropriate for the handle design of a tin opener in this range. For each criterion, explain why it is written in the way it is.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per design criterion). For each point: states a precise, measurable criterion (1 mark) e.g. 'The handle must require a grip force of no more than 20 N to operate'; explains why specificity matters in this context (1 mark) e.g. 'because vague criteria like comfortable cannot be tested or verified'; links to the user's need (1 mark) e.g. 'users with arthritis or reduced grip strength require defined force thresholds to ensure the product is genuinely accessible.' [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what gsm measures in relation to paper?
A) The physical thickness of the paper in millimetres
B) The number of sheets in a ream
C) The mass of one square metre of paper in grams
D) The ratio of paper width to height
practice_questions.marks: C) The mass of one square metre of paper in grams [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the dimensions of an A4 sheet of paper.
practice_questions.marks: 210 mm wide [1 mark] and 297 mm tall [1 mark]. (Both dimensions required for 2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Describe two properties of corrugated board that make it suitable for transit packaging.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks from:
• Rigid structure due to the fluted inner layer, which resists crushing [1]
• Lightweight relative to its thickness because the fluting creates air pockets [1]
• Provides cushioning and impact protection [1]
• Recyclable / made from recycled content [1]
(1 mark per valid property with brief reason; max 3)

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer might choose folding boxboard rather than plain card for a retail cereal box.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks from:
• Folding boxboard has a coated outer surface [1] which allows high-quality litho printing for graphics and branding [1]
• The multi-layer construction gives stiffness [1] so the box holds its shape on a shelf [1]
• The chemical-pulp outer layer produces a brighter white surface than mechanical pulp [1] which makes colours appear more vivid [1]
(2 marks per developed point; max 4)

practice_questions.text: Explain, with reference to a specific product, why manufacturers sometimes apply a laminate finish to printed board packaging. Include in your answer one potential disadvantage of laminating.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific product (e.g. paperback book cover, loyalty card, food carton), explains how laminating improves durability and water resistance in that context with a developed mechanism (e.g. polypropylene film prevents moisture penetration in a chilled food box), and evaluates a genuine disadvantage (e.g. laminate prevents the board from being recycled through standard paper streams, reducing end-of-life sustainability).
Secure: Names a product and explains one benefit of laminating with some product-specific detail, plus identifies one disadvantage.
Developing: General explanation of laminating benefits without product-specific application; disadvantage may be vague.
Emerging: Superficial statement about laminating with no product context or disadvantage.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using recycled paper rather than virgin-fibre paper for an office printing paper product. Consider both performance and environmental factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed points on both sides. Advantages may include: lower energy and water use in production, reduced demand on virgin timber, lower carbon footprint, can be certified under recognised schemes. Disadvantages may include: shorter fibre length reduces tensile strength with each recycle cycle, potential grey/cream tint reducing brightness, possible de-inking residues, OBAs harder to apply uniformly. Reaches a reasoned judgement about which factors weigh more heavily for the specific product context.
Secure: Two or more developed points on each side with some product-specific detail; judgement present but may lack full development.
Developing: Points identified on both sides but limited development; judgement weak or absent.
Emerging: Only one side addressed or points are superficial.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'technology push'?
A) Consumers demand a product that does not yet exist
B) Legislation forces manufacturers to change their products
C) A new scientific discovery creates products consumers had not asked for
D) A product reaches the decline stage of its life cycle
practice_questions.marks: C) A new scientific discovery creates products consumers had not asked for [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the four stages of the product life cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any two correct stages; two marks for all four:
• Introduction
• Growth
• Maturity
• Decline
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how global production can affect the design of a consumer product.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for developed points including:
• Components can be sourced from multiple countries, allowing designers to select the most cost-effective or highest-quality supplier (1 mark). This reduces production cost but can make quality control more complex (1 mark additional development).
• Designers must consider varying safety and environmental legislation in different export markets (1 mark).
• Cultural differences between markets may require design modifications to meet local preferences or requirements (1 mark).
[Max 3 marks; each developed point = 1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how consumer choice has influenced the development of electric vehicles. Refer to the concept of market pull in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
For each developed point award 2 marks (1 for basic point + 1 for development):
• Consumer concern about air quality and rising fuel costs created demand for cleaner transport before the technology was fully developed (1). Manufacturers invested in battery research because the market was pulling them towards a solution (1).
• Environmental legislation (e.g. emissions standards in cities) reinforced consumer demand by making petrol and diesel vehicles less attractive (1), accelerating investment in EV infrastructure and design (1).
[4 marks total; 2 marks per developed point]

practice_questions.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of designing products for a global market rather than a local one.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of advantages (economies of scale, wider consumer base, access to lower-cost components) and disadvantages (complex supply chains, ethical concerns over working conditions, need to meet multiple national standards). Reach a supported judgement about which factors matter most.
Secure: At least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with some specific context (e.g. a named material or sector).
Developing: Points made but limited development; mostly one side or both sides listed without balance.
Emerging: Simple statements with minimal explanation; no judgement reached.
[8 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text:
A sportswear manufacturer is considering using a new smart fabric that changes colour when the wearer overheats. The fabric has been developed by a research laboratory and is not yet widely available.

Evaluate whether introducing this new technology to the mass market is a realistic commercial decision for the manufacturer. Consider the product life cycle, market pull/technology push, consumer rights and legislation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Thorough evaluation linking technology push (lab development before demand), product life cycle (introduction phase risks), relevant legislation (safety/labelling requirements), and consumer willingness to pay. Reaches a justified, balanced conclusion with specific technical and commercial reasoning.
Secure: Addresses at least three of the four areas with development; clear conclusion though it may not be fully nuanced.
Developing: Two areas addressed with some development; conclusion present but unsupported.
Emerging: One or two simple points; no real evaluation or conclusion.
[10 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of the 'Repair' element of the 6 Rs?
A) Specifying thinner polymer walls to use less material
B) Using standard screws and publishing a service manual to extend product life
C) Sorting materials by type at end of life for recycling
D) Choosing a different product format that avoids the problem entirely
practice_questions.marks: B) Using standard screws and publishing a service manual to extend product life [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the four stages of a Life Cycle Analysis.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for two correct stages; two marks for all four:
• Raw material extraction
• Manufacturing
• Use phase
• End of life
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a designer could apply the 'Reduce' principle to the packaging of a children's toy.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for developed points:
• Reduce the thickness of the card box to use less material and lower the embodied energy of the packaging (1). This also reduces the weight of the shipped product, cutting transport emissions (1 additional development).
• Remove unnecessary inner trays or cable ties that add material without protecting the product (1).
• Replace plastic window inserts with a cut-out in the card so consumers can see the product without additional polymer (1).
[Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how Life Cycle Analysis helps a designer make more sustainable choices for a cotton T-shirt.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per developed point:
• LCA reveals that conventional cotton growing uses very large quantities of water and pesticides (1). This allows the designer to target raw material selection — specifying organic cotton or recycled polyester — rather than focusing only on packaging (1).
• The use phase may consume energy if the garment requires high-temperature washing (1). Designing for cold-wash compatibility (e.g. specifying fabrics that clean effectively at 30°C) reduces the lifetime energy footprint (1).
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of designing products using fair-trade certified materials.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of advantages (fair wages, safe working conditions, community investment, positive brand perception, social sustainability) and disadvantages (higher material cost, limited availability, supply chain complexity, potential greenwashing risk if not independently verified). Judgement reached about overall value.
Secure: Two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with some specific context; conclusion present.
Developing: Points made but imbalanced or underdeveloped; limited specific examples.
Emerging: Simple list of points with minimal explanation; no conclusion.
[8 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer produces a single-use plastic water bottle. Using the 6 Rs framework, evaluate what changes the designer could make to reduce the product's environmental impact. Refer to Life Cycle Analysis in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Thorough evaluation applying multiple 6 Rs with specific design actions (e.g. Rethink: switch to a reusable bottle format; Reduce: thin the polymer wall; Recycle: mark with correct polymer code and design for easy cap separation; Repair: not applicable — acknowledged and explained). LCA reference identifies which life cycle stage the change targets. Balanced judgement on feasibility and trade-offs.
Secure: At least three 6 Rs applied with development; LCA referenced meaningfully; conclusion present.
Developing: Two 6 Rs applied; LCA mentioned but not fully integrated; conclusion partially supported.
Emerging: One or two points; vague sustainability claims; no real evaluation.
[10 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text:
What is the area of an A0 sheet of paper?
A) 500 cm²
B) 1,000 cm²
C) 1 m²
D) 2 m²
practice_questions.marks: C) 1 m² [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two methods used to stiffen board for use in transit packaging.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: corrugation / lamination / correct grain direction orientation / multi-wall construction. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how corrugation increases the compressive strength of corrugated card.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
- The inner layer is formed into a fluted (wavy) shape between two flat liner sheets.
- The flutes act as a series of arches, distributing a downward compressive load across many small columns.
- This structure resists collapse under stacking loads far more effectively than a flat board of the same total weight. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer specifying packaging for a range of chilled ready meals might choose foil-lined board over standard folding boxboard.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Chilled ready meals contain moisture and require protection from oxygen to prevent spoilage, which standard folding boxboard cannot provide.
- Foil-lined board has an aluminium layer that acts as a barrier to both moisture vapour and oxygen, extending shelf life.
- The foil layer also provides a degree of insulation, helping to maintain the chilled temperature of the product during short periods outside refrigeration.
- Folding boxboard alone would allow moisture to migrate through the board, causing the carton to weaken and the product to deteriorate faster. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain, with reference to specific material properties, how a designer would select a board for a luxury perfume carton, considering both performance and aesthetic requirements.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Solid white board (SWB) would be selected for its brilliant white surface on both sides, ensuring that printed brand colours appear vivid and accurate.
- SWB is made entirely from bleached chemical pulp, giving it higher stiffness per unit of thickness than recycled-content boards, so the carton holds its shape on the shelf.
- A high-gloss or soft-touch laminate finish applied to the outer surface enhances the tactile quality of the carton, reinforcing the premium brand positioning.
- UV spot varnish or foil blocking on the logo adds a visual highlight that differentiates the product at point of sale.
- Cost is a secondary consideration for luxury packaging; the higher cost of SWB is justified by the elevated retail price of the perfume.
[6 marks - Mastering: Properties linked to both functional performance and aesthetic outcome with specific reference to the luxury context. Secure: Properties identified with some linkage to aesthetics or performance but without full development. Developing: Correct board named; limited justification. Emerging: Vague reference to quality only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of specifying recycled-content board for a food packaging carton, considering functional, aesthetic and environmental factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
- Using recycled fibre reduces the demand for virgin wood pulp, conserving forest resources and reducing carbon emissions associated with timber harvesting and chemical pulping.
- Recycled-content board can be certified and carry on-pack environmental claims (e.g. recycled content percentage) that appeal to eco-conscious consumers and major retailers.
- It is typically cheaper than virgin-fibre board, reducing the unit cost of the packaging and improving commercial viability.
- Recycled fibre can provide adequate structural performance for many food carton applications, such as cereal or cracker boxes, where extreme stiffness is not required.
Disadvantages:
- Shortened fibres in recycled board reduce tensile strength and stiffness, which can be a problem for packaging that must withstand heavy stacking in a warehouse.
- The grey or brown colour of recycled board requires a white-coated top surface to achieve a printable base, adding cost and reducing the net environmental benefit.
- Residual ink or contaminants in the recycled stream may affect food safety if the board is in direct contact with food, requiring an additional barrier liner.
- Consumer perception of recycled board as lower quality may undermine premium brand positioning for high-value food products.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion across functional, aesthetic and environmental dimensions with at least two developed points on each side. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

practice_questions.text:
What does PIC stand for in the context of electronic systems?
A) Printed Interface Circuit
B) Programmable Interface Controller
C) Passive Input Component
D) Processed Integrated Circuit
practice_questions.marks: B) Programmable Interface Controller [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two components found inside a microcontroller.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per correct component named, up to 2. Accept: processor/CPU; memory (flash/RAM); input/output pins. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a sub-routine is and explain why programmers use them.
practice_questions.marks:
• A sub-routine is a self-contained section of program code that performs a specific task. [1 mark]
• It can be called (used) from multiple points within the main program. [1 mark]
• This avoids repeating the same code, making programs shorter, easier to read and simpler to update. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a microcontroller's output pin cannot directly drive a motor and describe how this problem is solved.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A microcontroller's output pin can supply only a small current (around 20 to 40 mA), which is insufficient to drive a motor. [1 mark]
• A motor requires a much larger current to produce useful torque. [1 mark]
• A transistor or relay is connected between the output pin and the motor. [1 mark]
• The small current from the pin switches the transistor/relay on, which then allows the larger motor current to flow from a separate power supply. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A company manufactures a programmable security alarm that uses a microcontroller. Explain the advantages to the manufacturer of using a programmable system rather than a fixed circuit for this product.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The same circuit board can be programmed differently to produce a basic domestic alarm or a more complex commercial system, reducing tooling and manufacturing costs.
• Faults discovered after the product ships can be corrected by a software update rather than a product recall, saving significant cost.
• New features (e.g. an additional motion sensor input) can be added by updating the program without redesigning the hardware.
• The microcontroller replaces many discrete components, reducing board size and assembly time, which lowers unit cost.
[6 marks - Mastering: Three or more advantages with product-specific context developed. Secure: Two advantages with context. Developing: Two advantages named but context limited. Emerging: One advantage stated without development.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using a microcontroller rather than a fixed electronic circuit in a battery-powered children's toy.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
• The same toy can be updated with new sound effects or behaviours by reprogramming the microcontroller, extending the product's life without physical changes.
• One microcontroller replaces multiple discrete components, reducing board size and material cost, which is important in a price-sensitive toy market.
• If a programming fault causes the toy to behave incorrectly, a firmware update can fix it without recalling the product.
Disadvantages:
• A microcontroller consumes more power than a simple passive circuit, reducing battery life — a significant issue in a toy used by children who may forget to switch it off.
• Programming requires expertise; errors in the code could cause unexpected behaviour that might be perceived as a safety risk in a toy aimed at young children.
• For very simple functions (e.g. a sound that plays when a button is pressed), a fixed buzzer circuit would be cheaper and more reliable than a programmed microcontroller.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion, at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with battery-powered toy context throughout. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited context. Emerging: Superficial or one-sided response.]

practice_questions.text:
Which additive is mixed into PVC to make it flexible rather than rigid?
A) Flame retardant
B) UV stabiliser
C) Plasticiser
D) Pigment
practice_questions.marks: C) Plasticiser [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two stock forms in which polymers are supplied to manufacturers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct stock form up to 2. Accept: sheet, rod, tube, granules/powder, film/tape. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe why a designer might choose acrylic rather than polypropylene for a retail display sign.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Acrylic is optically clear, allowing the sign to transmit and display bright colours or backlighting effectively.
• Acrylic is self-finishing and weather-resistant, requiring no additional painting or protective coating outdoors.
• Polypropylene is more translucent and less optically clear than acrylic, making it less suitable for high-quality visual display. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what PLA is and why it is not a straightforward solution to plastic pollution.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• PLA (polylactic acid) is a biopolymer derived from fermented plant starch such as corn or sugarcane, not crude oil.
• It is industrially compostable under specific high-temperature conditions (58°C or above) but does not biodegrade in home compost or landfill.
• Growing crops for PLA requires land, water and agricultural chemicals, all carrying environmental costs.
• PLA can contaminate PET recycling streams if incorrectly sorted, reducing recycling efficiency for conventional plastics. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer would select a suitable polymer for the casing of a portable electric drill, considering function, aesthetics and environmental factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Function: the casing must be impact-resistant, rigid and electrically insulating — ABS is a strong candidate as it is tough, rigid, a good insulator and easy to form precisely by injection moulding.
Aesthetics: ABS is self-finishing and can be pigmented any colour, eliminating painting; its smooth surface accepts printed graphics for branding.
Environmental: ABS is recyclable (thermoforming), but injection moulding at scale uses significant energy; the designer might minimise wall thickness to reduce material use.
[6 marks — Mastering: function, aesthetics and environment all developed with ABS (or equivalent valid polymer) named and properties linked to drill-casing requirements. Secure: two criteria developed with named polymer. Developing: one criterion developed; polymer named but properties poorly linked. Emerging: general comments about plastic with no named polymer or specific properties.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using biopolymers such as PLA as replacements for conventional oil-based polymers in packaging.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages: renewable feedstock (corn/sugarcane) rather than finite crude oil; industrially compostable reducing landfill volume for food-contaminated packaging; similar optical clarity and rigidity to PET for packaging applications; growing interest and investment driving down cost.
Disadvantages: requires industrial composting infrastructure not universally available; does not biodegrade in landfill or home compost; crops require land, water and pesticides; contaminates PET recycling streams; currently more expensive than commodity polymers such as PET; physical properties (heat resistance, moisture barrier) often inferior to oil-based equivalents.
[8 marks — Mastering: sustained, balanced discussion; at least two developed points per side with examples such as food packaging or 3D printing; evaluates whether the benefits are achievable in practice given infrastructure limitations. Secure: two points per side with some development. Developing: points listed with limited development; unbalanced. Emerging: superficial one-sided response.]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a hardwood?
A) Scots pine
B) Western red cedar
C) Parana pine
D) Mahogany
practice_questions.marks: D) Mahogany [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the timber defect that occurs when cracks run along the grain following the annual growth rings.
practice_questions.marks: Ring shake [2 marks]. (Accept: shake [1 mark] with no specification of type.)

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which MDF differs from solid timber that make it suitable for painted furniture components.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks from:
• MDF has a uniform, grain-free surface that takes paint smoothly without visible grain showing through [1]
• MDF does not warp, cup or twist as solid timber can when moisture levels change [1]
• MDF is produced in large, consistent sheet sizes (typically 2440 × 1220 mm) with no knots or natural defects [1]
• MDF can be cut and routed to precise profiles and edges without splitting [1]
(1 mark per valid point; max 3)

practice_questions.text: Explain why jelutong is preferred over oak for producing prototype models in a design studio.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks from:
• Jelutong is a fine, uniform-grained timber [1] that can be cut, carved and sanded to precise shapes accurately [1]
• Oak is a dense, hard timber [1] that requires more effort and specialist tools to work accurately at small model scales [1]
• Jelutong takes adhesives cleanly and can be painted or primed easily for presentation [1]
• Oak’s coarse grain would show through paint finishes on fine-detail models [1]
(2 marks per developed comparative point; max 4)

practice_questions.text: A furniture manufacturer is designing a garden bench to be sold without surface treatment. Explain, with reference to the material’s properties, why western red cedar is a more suitable timber choice than Scots pine for this application.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies western red cedar’s phenolic oils as the source of its natural rot resistance, explains how this removes the need for chemical preservative treatment (cost and environmental benefit), compares Scots pine’s need for pressure treatment to withstand outdoor conditions, and links the material properties directly to the product context (untreated garden bench).
Secure: Explains that cedar is naturally rot-resistant and pine needs treatment for outdoor use, with some material-property detail.
Developing: States cedar is more durable outdoors without explaining the mechanism or product context sufficiently.
Emerging: Vague statement that cedar is ‘better for outside’ with no property-based reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using plywood rather than solid oak for the seat and back panels of a dining chair. Consider structural performance, aesthetics, cost and sustainability.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed points on both sides across multiple criteria. Advantages of plywood: consistent dimensions with no warping risk; cross-grain lamination gives strength in multiple directions; can be bent into curved profiles using steam or formers; typically cheaper per board metre than solid oak; can use thin oak face veneer for aesthetic appearance. Disadvantages: edge appearance is unattractive unless lipped; structural grades have visible layers; cannot be re-surfaced by sanding as many times as solid oak; relies on adhesives whose performance degrades. Reaches a reasoned judgement about which set of factors weighs more heavily for the dining chair context.
Secure: Two or more developed points on each side with some product-relevant detail; judgement present.
Developing: Points on both sides identified but limited development; judgement weak.
Emerging: Mainly one side addressed or points superficial.

practice_questions.text:
Which weave structure creates a diagonal rib on the fabric surface?
A) Plain weave
B) Satin weave
C) Twill weave
D) Warp knit
practice_questions.marks: C) Twill weave [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the two sets of yarns used to make a woven fabric.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each: warp (yarns running lengthways) and weft (yarns running widthways). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a knitted fabric differs from a woven fabric in terms of its structure and stretch properties.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• A knitted fabric is made from interlocking loops formed from a single yarn, whereas a woven fabric interlaces two sets of yarns (warp and weft) at right angles.
• The looped structure of a knitted fabric allows it to stretch easily in multiple directions.
• A woven fabric is relatively stable and does not stretch significantly along the warp or weft grain. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why felt is used for craft projects rather than woven fabrics, referring to its structure and properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Felt is a non-woven fabric made by matting wool fibres together; its structure means it does not have a warp and weft, so it does not fray when cut.
• This means edges do not need to be hemmed or finished, making it quicker and easier to use for cutting intricate shapes.
• Felt is also relatively inexpensive and available in a range of colours, making it accessible for craft use.
• Its thickness and stiffness allow it to hold a cut shape without curling or distorting.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer would select an appropriate fabric for a high-performance cycling jersey, considering at least three different criteria.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Function: the fabric must have stretch and recovery to allow freedom of movement; a weft-knit structure with elastane would provide this. It should also manage moisture (wick sweat away) to keep the rider comfortable at high exertion levels.
• Function: aerodynamic properties may be needed — a smooth, low-drag surface fabric reduces wind resistance at speed.
• Aesthetics: bright, visually distinctive colours or team livery are important for visibility and branding; the fabric must accept vibrant dye.
• Cost: professional cycling jerseys use high-specification technical fabrics (e.g. engineered polyester-elastane blends), which cost more but the target market (professional or serious amateur cyclists) will pay a premium.
• Environment: a manufacturer might choose recycled polyester (rPET) to reduce environmental impact without compromising performance.
[6 marks — Mastering: Three or more criteria addressed with specific fabric/construction choices and clear justification. Secure: Three criteria named with some development. Developing: Two criteria with limited development. Emerging: One criterion or very vague answer.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of woven fabrics compared with knitted fabrics for a fashion designer producing a range of tailored suits.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of woven fabrics for tailored suits:
• Woven fabrics (e.g. twill-weave wool gabardine) are dimensionally stable — they hold their shape and do not stretch out during wear, essential for a structured jacket silhouette.
• They can be cut and manipulated using tailoring techniques (darts, pad stitching, interfacing) that depend on the fabric not distorting.
• A wide range of yarns, thread counts and weave structures allow the designer to select specific weights and textures for summer or winter wear.
Disadvantages of woven fabrics for tailored suits:
• Woven fabrics fray when cut, requiring all seam allowances and edges to be finished, adding time and cost to construction.
• They offer minimal comfort stretch; a poorly fitted woven suit restricts movement, so fit must be precise.
Advantages of knitted fabrics for tailored suits:
• Knitted fabrics (e.g. ponte knit) offer inherent stretch, meaning the suit is more comfortable across a range of body movements and sizes without needing darts for ease.
• Knit suits are often lighter and more packable, appealing to business travellers.
Disadvantages of knitted fabrics for tailored suits:
• Knits can bag at the knees and elbows and are harder to press into crisp lines, making the garment look less formal over time.
• Many knit structures snag or ladder, shortening the product's life.
[8 marks — Mastering: Balanced, developed discussion with at least two points per side linked clearly to the tailored suit context. Secure: Points identified with some development and reasonable balance. Developing: Listed points, limited context or imbalanced. Emerging: One-sided or superficial.]

practice_questions.text: Identify the designer most associated with the philosophy that aesthetics should be a product's primary function.
practice_questions.marks: Philippe Starck [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the product that made James Dyson's reputation and the principle behind its design.
practice_questions.marks: Product: the bagless vacuum cleaner (DC01 / G-Force) [1 mark]. Principle: cyclonic separation — separating dust from air without a bag so suction is not lost [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how Apple's choice of materials in its laptop range reflects its design philosophy.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Credit: MacBook body machined from a single billet of aluminium (1 mark); this communicates durability and premium quality through material choice alone (1 mark); reflects Apple's philosophy of minimalism and precision — removing seams, ports and separate components wherever possible (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the design of the Airbus A380 demonstrates the importance of materials selection in large-scale engineering.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Identifies the material (carbon fibre reinforced polymer composites replacing aluminium in structural sections) [1 mark]; explains the property advantage (lower density than aluminium, reducing aircraft weight) [1 mark]; links to a performance outcome (reduced fuel consumption per passenger, enabling the A380 to meet stringent emission limits) [1 mark]; contextualises within Airbus philosophy (every material decision is driven by measurable performance data and safety regulation rather than aesthetic preference) [1 mark]. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the design philosophies of James Dyson and Philippe Starck. In your answer, refer to at least one specific product from each designer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks. Dyson: problem-led, seeks to eliminate accepted performance compromises through iterative prototyping (e.g. DC01 bagless vacuum eliminates loss of suction) [1 mark + development 1 mark]. Starck: prioritises aesthetic impact and emotional response over functional efficiency (e.g. Juicy Salif deliberately sacrifices juicing efficiency to create a sculptural conversation piece) [1 mark + development 1 mark]. Comparison point: both designers reject conventional solutions, but Dyson rethinks function while Starck rethinks purpose [1 mark]. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that a designer's visual identity is more important than engineering performance in creating commercially successful products. Refer to at least two of the named designers in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument developed across both sides. Arguments for visual identity (Williamson's bold colour palette translates his brand across fashion and homeware; Starck's Juicy Salif sells on visual impact despite being an inefficient juicer; Apple's minimalist aesthetic drives brand loyalty beyond product functionality). Arguments for engineering performance (Dyson's products succeed because they solve real problems other manufacturers ignored; Airbus competes on measurable safety, efficiency and capacity targets; a product with a distinctive look but poor function will eventually fail commercially). Strong conclusion weighing both factors, e.g. neither alone suffices — Dyson's success required both a genuine performance breakthrough and a product that looked distinctive on the shop floor. Secure: Both sides present, limited conclusion. Developing: One side only. Emerging: General points without designer reference. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which heat treatment process produces the softest, most ductile result in steel?
A) Hardening
B) Tempering
C) Annealing
D) Case hardening
practice_questions.marks: C) Annealing [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two stock forms in which aluminium is commercially supplied.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: sheet / plate / bar / rod / tube / angle section. Must be standard stock forms. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to mild steel during work hardening.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• When mild steel is repeatedly bent or cold-worked, dislocations build up in its crystal structure.
• This makes the metal progressively harder.
• However, the metal also becomes less ductile (more brittle) and will eventually crack or fracture if deformation continues. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the hardening process must always be followed by tempering.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hardening (heating then rapid quenching) produces a very hard but extremely brittle crystal structure in the steel.
• A hardened but untempered steel would fracture under impact or shock loading, making it unsuitable for most applications.
• Tempering reheats the hardened steel to a lower temperature (150-400°C), which relieves internal stresses and allows some ductility to return.
• The result is a steel that retains much of its hardness while gaining enough toughness to withstand the forces in service, e.g. a chisel blade that cuts without shattering.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why case hardening is used for the gear teeth of a bicycle gearbox rather than simply using high carbon steel throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Gear teeth need a very hard, wear-resistant surface to withstand repeated metal-to-metal contact without deteriorating.
• The core of the gear must be tough enough to absorb the shock loads transmitted by rapid gear changes without fracturing.
• High carbon steel throughout would be hard but brittle: the entire gear, including the root of each tooth, would be at risk of sudden fracture under impact.
• Case hardening on mild steel addresses both requirements: the surface is enriched with carbon and quenched to produce a hard case, while the mild steel core remains tough and ductile.
• This combination extends product life and improves safety compared to a uniformly hard but brittle gear.
[6 marks — Mastering: Both surface and core requirements explained, mechanism of case hardening described, compared to alternative with reference to product context. Secure: Both requirements and the process described but comparison limited. Developing: Process described but link to product requirements thin. Emerging: Superficial reference to hardening without explaining the case/core distinction.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using titanium rather than mild steel for the frame of a high-performance bicycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of titanium:
• Titanium has an exceptional strength-to-weight ratio; a titanium frame can be as strong as steel at a fraction of the mass, reducing overall bicycle weight and improving performance.
• Titanium is highly corrosion resistant without any surface treatment, making it suitable for use in wet, muddy and salty conditions without rusting.
• Titanium has a degree of flex that can provide a more comfortable ride than the stiffer steel alternative.
• Long service life means less frequent replacement; over a lifetime the higher initial cost may be offset.
Disadvantages of titanium:
• Titanium costs approximately 50 times more per kilogram than mild steel, making titanium frames prohibitively expensive for most consumers.
• Titanium is significantly more difficult to machine and weld; it must be welded in an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, requiring specialist equipment and skilled labour, further increasing cost.
• Titanium is less readily available than mild steel, making repairs in the field or by a local welder less practical.
• Mild steel frames can be easily repaired, reshaped and sourced cheaply; this is a significant advantage for budget and touring cyclists.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages, linked to bicycle performance and manufacturing context. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; limited balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial.]

practice_questions.text:
Which stock form of timber is sold with a rough sawn surface at nominal dimensions?
A) PAR
B) PSE
C) Sawn timber
D) Moulding
practice_questions.marks: C) Sawn timber [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two functional criteria a designer must consider when selecting timber for an outdoor garden bench.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: moisture resistance / rot resistance / durability outdoors / strength / hardness / ease of finishing with preservative. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a hygroscopic material and explain why this is a problem for solid timber products.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• A hygroscopic material absorbs and releases moisture from the surrounding air, causing it to change dimensions.
• As moisture content increases, timber swells; as it decreases, timber shrinks, and the movement is unequal in different grain directions.
• This uneven movement causes warping, cupping, twisting or joint failure in a finished product if the timber was not properly seasoned or the design does not accommodate movement. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a manufacturer of flat-pack bedroom furniture would specify chipboard covered with a melamine finish rather than solid oak.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Chipboard is produced in large, consistent sheet sizes so components can be efficiently cut by CNC machinery with minimal waste, reducing production cost.
• Chipboard is significantly cheaper than solid oak, making the finished furniture more affordable for a mass market.
• Melamine laminate applied to the chipboard surface provides a durable, wipe-clean surface without the need for additional finishing, reducing labour costs.
• Chipboard is more dimensionally stable than solid oak, so the cabinet panels will not move or warp with seasonal humidity changes, keeping joints tight.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how lamination is used to overcome the limitations of solid timber in the construction of a curved chair backrest. Include reference to the forces acting on the component in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Thin strips of timber (laminates) are bent around a curved jig and bonded with adhesive; the adhesive locks the curve in place when cured, creating a permanently curved component without the waste of cutting a curve from solid timber.
• Because the grain of each laminate follows the curve, the finished component has no short grain running across the section, so it resists bending forces more effectively than a solid curved piece would.
• The chair backrest must resist bending (the user leaning against it), compression and tension simultaneously; the laminated construction spreads these stresses across many bonded glue lines rather than depending on a single grain direction.
• Lamination also reduces hygroscopic movement because adjacent layers resist each other's tendency to expand and contract, giving a more stable component than solid timber.
[6 marks — Mastering: Both construction process and structural behaviour explained with applied force analysis. Secure: Process and stability advantage explained but force analysis limited. Developing: Process described without structural explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to lamination.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of specifying PAR (Planed All Round) timber rather than sawn timber for a batch of workshop-made dining chairs.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
• PAR timber has smooth, accurately dimensioned faces so no further planing is needed before assembly, saving time and labour on each chair.
• The consistent dimensions of PAR timber reduce the need for individual measurement and adjustment at each joint, improving accuracy in batch production.
• A smooth surface takes adhesive and finish more uniformly, improving joint strength and aesthetic quality of the painted or varnished finish.
• PAR timber presents a professional appearance in any exposed component, avoiding the need for additional finishing steps.
Disadvantages:
• PAR timber costs more per metre than sawn timber because of the additional processing involved in planing.
• The actual dimensions of PAR timber are smaller than the nominal size; a designer who fails to account for this may produce components that are slightly shorter than intended, requiring design drawings to use actual rather than nominal sizes.
• PAR timber sourced from a supplier may have a surface wax or contamination that must be removed before gluing, or the glue joint may fail.
• For structural components hidden inside the frame of the chair, the additional cost of PAR over sawn timber adds expense with no functional benefit.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages applied to chair-making context. Secure: Two of each with some development. Developing: Limited development or imbalanced. Emerging: Superficial or one-sided.]

practice_questions.text:
Which cutting method uses a focused beam to cut fabric precisely, sealing synthetic edges at the same time?
A) Fabric shears
B) Rotary cutter
C) Die cutting
D) Laser cutter
practice_questions.marks: D) Laser cutter [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two methods used to mark pattern piece information onto fabric before cutting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: tailor's chalk, tracing wheel and dressmaker's carbon paper, tailor's tacks, fabric marker pen. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a French seam is made and explain one reason it is used on fine fabrics.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• The fabric pieces are placed wrong sides together and stitched just outside the finished seam line.
• The seam is trimmed, the fabric is turned so right sides are together, and a second line of stitching encloses all raw edges within the fold.
• This is used on fine, sheer fabrics such as silk because it leaves no visible raw edges that would fray or show through the delicate fabric. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a flat fell seam is the most suitable choice for constructing the inner leg seam of a pair of denim jeans.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A flat fell seam is sewn twice, giving double the strength — essential for a seam that is under repeated stress and tension as the wearer walks or runs.
• It lies flat, which is important for comfort on the inner leg where a bulky or raised seam would cause chafing.
• It encloses all raw edges completely, preventing fraying through repeated machine washing.
• The two visible rows of topstitching are characteristic of denim construction and are aesthetically expected by consumers.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the choice of cutting method affects the quality and efficiency of production for a manufacturer making 5,000 identical pocket linings per day.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
