• At a volume of 5,000 per day, die cutting is the most efficient method: a shaped metal die cuts through many fabric layers simultaneously, producing identical shapes in seconds with no repositioning of a pattern.
• Die cutting ensures absolute consistency in shape and size — critical for pockets that must align precisely with the pocket opening in every garment.
• Laser cutting could also achieve high precision but is slower than die cutting at this volume and has a higher running cost per item.
• Using fabric shears at this volume would be impractical: slow speed, high labour cost and human variation in each cut would introduce unacceptable inconsistency.
• A laser cutter would add value if the pocket shape were intricate or if the fabric were synthetic (the laser seals the cut edge, removing a separate finishing step).
[6 marks — Mastering: Die cutting justified in full for this context plus comparison to at least one alternative with clear reasoning. Secure: Die cutting selected with justification; limited comparison. Developing: Appropriate method identified with partial justification. Emerging: Method named without development or wrong method selected.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using a laser cutter compared with traditional cutting methods (shears and die cutting) when a small fashion design studio produces bespoke wedding dresses.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of laser cutting for bespoke wedding dresses:
• Extreme precision allows intricate lace patterns, decorative cut-outs and complex petal shapes that would be impossible or very time-consuming with shears.
• The laser is computer-controlled from a digital pattern, reducing human error and enabling minor size adjustments without making new paper patterns.
• For synthetic fabrics (e.g. polyester satin lining), the laser seals edges as it cuts, eliminating a separate overlock step and saving time on each dress.
Disadvantages of laser cutting for bespoke wedding dresses:
• Capital cost of a laser cutter is high — a small studio making only a few dresses per week may not be able to justify the investment compared with skilled hand-cutting.
• Laser cutting can leave a slight scorched edge on some natural fabrics (silk, cotton) and may cause discolouration on delicate, pale-coloured bridal fabrics — unacceptable for a premium product.
• Not all laser-cuttable machines handle thick, multilayered fabrics (e.g. structured bodice with interlining) as well as a skilled cutter using shears.
Comparison with die cutting:
• Die cutting is unsuitable for bespoke one-off production because each die is expensive to make and only economical for high-volume identical shapes — the opposite of one-of-a-kind wedding dresses.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion with at least two developed points per side linked to the bespoke wedding dress context; meaningful comparison with die cutting. Secure: At least two points per side with some development. Developing: Points listed, limited development, some imbalance. Emerging: Superficial or one-sided.]

practice_questions.text:
Which commercial process uses a steel-rule die to cut and crease a carton net in a single operation?
A) Guillotining
B) Kiss cutting
C) Die cutting
D) Laser cutting
practice_questions.marks: C) Die cutting [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two types of rule found in a die-cutting die and state the purpose of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each: cutting rule — a sharp rule that cuts cleanly through the board / creasing rule — a blunt, slightly lower rule that compresses the fibres to form a fold line without cutting through. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how laser cutting is used to shape a net from a sheet of board.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
- A focused CO2 laser beam vaporises or burns through the board along a digitally defined path.
- The cutting path is defined in software with no physical tooling required, so designs can be changed instantly.
- The laser can cut complex curves and shapes to high precision, making it suitable for prototyping and short production runs. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a packaging manufacturer would choose die cutting rather than laser cutting for producing one million cereal carton nets.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Die cutting cuts and creases the entire net in a single press stroke, allowing tens of thousands of sheets to be processed per hour.
- At one million units, the high initial cost of making the steel-rule die is spread across a large number of cartons, making the per-unit cost very low.
- Laser cutting processes one sheet at a time along a sequential path, making it far too slow and expensive per unit for high-volume production.
- Die cutting produces consistent, repeatable results across every sheet without operator adjustment, which is essential for cartons that must be assembled automatically by folding-and-gluing machines. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain what kiss cutting is, how it works and why it is used for self-adhesive product labels. Include a description of the process and its advantages.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Kiss cutting is a form of die cutting where the blade is set to a precise depth that cuts through the face paper and adhesive layer but does not penetrate the backing paper.
- The cutting depth must be controlled to within fractions of a millimetre to avoid cutting the backing and losing the integrity of the roll or sheet of labels.
- The result is a label that is fully cut to shape but remains attached to the backing paper, allowing it to be peeled off cleanly when needed.
- The intact backing paper allows the labels to be wound into rolls and fed through automatic labelling machines at high speed without the labels separating prematurely.
- Compared with full die cutting, kiss cutting eliminates the need for the user to cut or separate labels individually, reducing application time and wastage.
[6 marks - Mastering: Full explanation of mechanism, depth control and product application with advantages clearly linked. Secure: Mechanism and application explained but advantages limited. Developing: Correct definition with some process detail; limited application. Emerging: Partial definition only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using laser cutting compared with die cutting for producing packaging nets in a small design studio.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of laser cutting:
- No tooling cost: the cutting path is defined entirely in software, so there is no need to invest in a steel-rule die, which can cost hundreds of pounds.
- Designs can be modified instantly between cuts, making it ideal for iterative prototyping where the net shape is still being refined.
- Capable of cutting intricate curves and complex shapes that would be difficult or expensive to produce with a die.
- A single machine can cut and engrave different jobs without any changeover time.
Disadvantages of laser cutting:
- Slow throughput: the laser traces each cutting path sequentially, making it impractical for production quantities above a few hundred units.
- Charring and burn marks on cut edges can affect the appearance of light-coloured or white boards, requiring sanding or masking.
- The machine has a high purchase and maintenance cost, although shared facilities (e.g. a school workshop or fabrication lab) reduce the per-use cost.
- Cutting thicker boards (e.g. 5 mm foam board) may require multiple passes, reducing accuracy and increasing processing time.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages relevant to a small design studio context. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following energy sources is non-renewable?
A) Solar
B) Biomass
C) Natural gas
D) Hydroelectric
practice_questions.marks: C) Natural gas [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using solar (photovoltaic) cells to power a garden lighting product.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per advantage (any two):
• No running cost once installed (no mains electricity needed)
• No direct CO2 emissions during operation
• No wiring required — can be placed anywhere with sufficient sunlight
• Battery can be charged during the day and power lights at night
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a wind-up mechanism stores and releases energy in a product.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Turning the winding key stores mechanical (potential) energy in a coiled spring (1).
• When released, the spring uncoils and transfers kinetic energy to the mechanism (1).
• This energy can drive a generator to produce electricity or directly power moving parts (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer might choose to power a portable music device using a lithium-ion battery rather than disposable alkaline batteries.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per developed point:
• Lithium-ion batteries have a higher energy density than alkaline batteries (1), meaning the device can operate for longer between charges without increasing the product’s size or weight (1).
• Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable and can complete hundreds of charge cycles (1), reducing running costs and the number of batteries sent to landfill compared with single-use alkaline cells (1).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer of children's toys is deciding whether to power its products using disposable batteries or rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. Explain, with reference to energy storage and sustainability, which option a designer would be justified in recommending.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed argument for the justified recommendation, with specific reference to energy density, rechargeability, lifecycle cost and disposal/recycling implications for both types. The toy context is embedded (e.g. child-safe charging, product lifespan).
Secure: Both options considered with developed points; recommendation clearly linked to sustainability and storage properties.
Developing: Basic comparison made; sustainability mentioned but not specifically linked to storage type.
Emerging: Simple statements about batteries being better or worse; minimal technical reasoning.
[6 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using wind power as an energy source for national electricity generation compared with nuclear power.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation covering wind advantages (renewable, zero emissions during operation, scalable, no radioactive waste) and disadvantages (intermittent, visual impact, noise, requires storage or grid balancing), versus nuclear advantages (reliable baseload, low direct emissions, high energy density) and disadvantages (radioactive waste, long construction time, accident risk, high decommissioning cost). Weighted judgement reached.
Secure: At least two developed points per source; judgement present.
Developing: Points mostly listed without development; one side stronger than the other.
Emerging: Simple pros/cons with minimal explanation; no judgement.
[8 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following metals is non-ferrous?
A) Cast iron
B) Mild steel
C) High carbon steel
D) Copper
practice_questions.marks: D) Copper [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term ductility in relation to metals.
practice_questions.marks: The ability of a material to be drawn into wire or thin sections without breaking [2 marks]. (1 mark for partial answer: ‘can be stretched’ without further qualification.)

practice_questions.text: Identify the two metals that are combined to produce brass, and describe one property that makes brass suitable for plumbing fittings.
practice_questions.marks: Copper [1] and zinc [1]. One mark for a relevant property with brief reason, e.g. brass is corrosion-resistant so it does not degrade in contact with water [1], or brass is non-sparking so it is safe around gases [1], or brass machines cleanly for precision threaded fittings [1]. (3 marks total.)

practice_questions.text: Explain why tube is often preferred over solid round bar for cycle frame construction, even though both are the same material.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks from:
• Tube provides a high strength-to-weight ratio [1] because material is placed at maximum distance from the neutral axis, making bending resistance high relative to mass [1]
• Solid bar of the same diameter would be much heavier [1] which would reduce performance and increase energy required to accelerate the bike [1]
• Tube can be butted (thicker at stress points, thinner in the middle) to further optimise material use [1]
(2 marks per developed point; max 4)

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is producing mild steel garden furniture for sale without any surface finish. Explain, with reference to the product’s function and environment, why this is problematic and recommend a suitable finishing process, justifying your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that mild steel contains iron and will rust in outdoor conditions where moisture and oxygen are present, degrading the structure and appearance over time. Recommends a specific finish (e.g. powder coating) with justified reasoning linking the finish mechanism to the product context (electrostatically applied polymer cures to a durable, weather-resistant surface available in a wide colour range; more durable than liquid paint and produces less VOC). Mentions that galvanising is an alternative for structural outdoor steel.
Secure: Identifies the rust problem and recommends a named finish with some explanation of the mechanism.
Developing: States mild steel rusts and recommends ‘painting’ without explaining surface preparation or process.
Emerging: Identifies that the metal will corrode but cannot name or explain a finishing method.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using aluminium rather than mild steel for a bicycle frame. Consider material properties, processing and environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed points on both sides. Aluminium advantages: density ~2.7 g/cm³ vs steel ~7.8 g/cm³ gives significantly lower mass; naturally corrosion-resistant so no protective finish needed (cost and environmental saving); can be anodised for decorative effect; high recycled content possible. Aluminium disadvantages: lower tensile strength per unit volume than steel (aluminium ~100–300 MPa vs mild steel ~400–500 MPa) so larger cross-sections or alloy grades needed; aluminium work-hardens and can crack under repeated fatigue loading; welding aluminium requires specialist TIG process and inert shielding gas. Reaches a reasoned judgement.
Secure: Two or more developed points on each side with property-specific detail; judgement present.
Developing: Points on both sides but limited development.
Emerging: Mainly one side or superficial.

practice_questions.text:
Which manufacturing process is most suitable for making a large hollow water storage tank from LDPE?
A) Injection moulding
B) Vacuum forming
C) Compression moulding
D) Rotational moulding
practice_questions.marks: D) Rotational moulding [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the shaping process used for thermosetting polymers such as urea formaldehyde, and briefly describe how it works.
practice_questions.marks: Compression moulding [1 mark]. Accept a brief description of the process for the second mark: a charge of resin is placed in a heated mould and pressed into shape by a matching upper tool / the material cures permanently inside the mould. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of vacuum forming a thermoforming polymer sheet.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• A sheet of thermoforming polymer (e.g. HIPS) is clamped and heated until it softens.
• The softened sheet is drawn or lowered over a mould and air is pumped out from beneath, creating a vacuum.
• The sheet is drawn tightly against the mould surface, cooled and then removed and trimmed to produce the final shape. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why injection moulding is used for high-volume production of ABS components such as computer mouse shells, rather than vacuum forming.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Injection moulding can produce fully three-dimensional, complex internal and external features in a single operation, whereas vacuum forming only produces shallow, open-topped shapes.
• Injection moulding delivers very high dimensional accuracy and excellent surface finish, suitable for the precise fit of a computer mouse shell.
• Although injection mould tooling is expensive, the cost per part at high volumes (hundreds of thousands of units) is very low.
• Vacuum forming would produce a shell with uniform wall thickness only from above, cannot form ribs or internal features, and requires additional assembly steps. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why 3D printing is preferred over injection moulding for producing a one-off prototype of a new polymer product.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
No tooling cost: injection moulding requires a precision steel mould costing thousands of pounds; 3D printing needs only a digital file and filament costing a few pounds.
Speed of iteration: a 3D-printed prototype can be modified digitally and reprinted within hours; a revised injection mould takes weeks to machine.
Complex geometry: 3D printing can produce internal lattices, overhangs and complex channels without additional cost; injection moulding requires draft angles and cannot easily produce undercuts.
Limitations of 3D printing: slower build speed, visible layer lines (lower surface finish), and weaker mechanical properties along layer boundaries — making it unsuitable for production at scale.
[6 marks — Mastering: both advantages and limitations developed with specific process details and prototype context. Secure: advantages well covered, limitations briefly noted. Developing: advantages listed with limited justification; limitations absent. Emerging: one-sided, superficial comparison.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of injection moulding compared with vacuum forming for manufacturing polymer components.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of injection moulding: fully 3D complex shapes with internal features; high dimensional accuracy; excellent surface finish; very low unit cost at high volumes; suitable for a wide range of thermoforming polymers.
Disadvantages of injection moulding: very high tooling (mould) cost; long lead time to produce tool; high minimum volumes to be economical; not suitable for thermosets.
Advantages of vacuum forming: low tooling cost (moulds can be MDF or aluminium); quick to set up; good for shallow packaging and medium volumes; accessible for small batch production.
Disadvantages of vacuum forming: limited to shallow, open forms; cannot produce complex internal features or enclosed shapes; wall thickness is uneven (thinner at sharp corners); trimming waste generated.
[8 marks — Mastering: sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed points per side, specific examples (e.g. LEGO brick vs yoghurt pot tray), and consideration of economic factors. Secure: two points per side with development. Developing: points listed with limited development; unbalanced. Emerging: one-sided or very superficial.]

practice_questions.text:
Which sawing method produces quarter-sawn timber with medullary ray figure visible on the face?
A) Through-and-through sawing
B) Ripping along the grain
C) Band-saw re-sawing
D) Quarter sawing
practice_questions.marks: D) Quarter sawing [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two hand tools used to mark out timber accurately before cutting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: try square / marking gauge / mortise gauge / marking knife / sliding bevel / steel rule. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the process a student would follow to use a tenon saw to cut the shoulder of a mortise-and-tenon joint accurately.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Mark the shoulder line clearly with a marking knife and try square from the face edge, and mark the waste side.
• Secure the timber in a bench hook or vice so the shoulder line is visible and the saw can run freely.
• Begin the cut with a backward pull stroke to establish a groove at the line, then use steady forward strokes keeping the saw horizontal and on the waste side of the line. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the advantages of using a CNC router rather than a hand router for producing 200 identical curved cabinet door panels.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A CNC router follows a digital file precisely, producing each panel to a tolerance of ±0.1 mm, so all 200 panels will be identical without any variation introduced by the operator.
• The CAD/CAM nesting software arranges panels on each sheet to minimise off-cuts, reducing material waste and cost across a large batch.
• Once programmed, the CNC router runs unattended, freeing the operator for other tasks and greatly reducing labour costs per unit.
• Complex curved profiles can be cut in a single pass without repositioning the workpiece, reducing handling time and the risk of error.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between through-and-through sawing and quarter sawing, including why a furniture maker would choose quarter-sawn oak for a dining table top. Refer to relevant properties in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Through-and-through sawing cuts the log in parallel slices; it is fast and economical but produces boards from the outer log with growth rings at a low angle to the face, making them prone to cupping as moisture content changes.
• Quarter sawing cuts radially through each quarter of the log; the growth rings are at 60-90° to the face, which significantly reduces cupping and warping and produces the distinctive medullary ray silver figure in oak.
• For a dining table top, dimensional stability is critical: a cupped or warped top is both visually and functionally unacceptable, and quarter-sawn oak's superior stability avoids this.
• The medullary ray figure in quarter-sawn oak is aesthetically prized in quality furniture, adding commercial value and visual interest to the finished tabletop.
• Quarter-sawn timber commands a higher price because of increased waste and processing time, which is justified in a premium dining table where appearance and longevity are key selling points.
[6 marks — Mastering: Both processes explained with grain direction detail, and choice justified with linked stability and aesthetic arguments. Secure: Both methods described and choice justified but technical grain detail limited. Developing: One method described or choice made without justification. Emerging: Vague or confused response.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using a wood lathe to produce a batch of 50 turned chair legs compared with using a CNC router to cut identically shaped legs.
practice_questions.marks:
Lathe advantages:
• A lathe can produce fully round, cylindrical and sculptural three-dimensional forms that a CNC router cannot replicate; a turned spindle has a true circular cross-section.
• For bespoke or small-batch work, the lathe requires minimal setup time; a skilled turner can produce a leg rapidly without programming time.
• Lathe-turned products have a handcrafted quality and slight variation that some markets (antique reproduction, craft furniture) value over machine uniformity.
Lathe disadvantages:
• Each leg requires an individual skilled operator, making the process slow and expensive for a batch of 50; labour cost per unit is high.
• Consistent reproduction of identical profiles by hand is difficult; small variations between legs may be visible in the finished batch.
• The lathe presents significant safety risks (tool catches, unsecured blanks) requiring trained operators and supervision.
CNC router advantages:
• Once the design file is programmed, the router reproduces each leg to ±0.1 mm accuracy across the entire batch of 50 with no operator variation.
• Production speed is much higher; multiple legs can be nested on a single sheet of laminated timber and cut in one session.
CNC router disadvantages:
• A standard 3-axis CNC router cannot produce a fully round turned profile in one pass; additional axes (4-axis or 5-axis CNC) are needed, significantly increasing equipment cost.
• High setup and programming costs make CNC less economical for very small batches where a skilled lathe operator could match total time.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages for each method, applied to chair-leg production. Secure: Two of each with some development. Developing: Limited development or imbalanced. Emerging: Superficial or one-sided.]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the 'Define' phase of the Double Diamond design process?
A) Generating a wide range of possible solutions
B) Gathering evidence about users and the context without filtering
C) Narrowing research findings into a clear problem statement
D) Testing and refining a final prototype
practice_questions.marks: C) Narrowing research findings into a clear problem statement [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by design fixation.
practice_questions.marks: Design fixation is when a designer becomes attached to an early idea (1 mark) and stops genuinely exploring alternative solutions as a result (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how systems thinking could be applied when designing a new electric bicycle for urban commuters.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Credit: considers how the bicycle interacts with urban charging infrastructure (1 mark); examines how the battery management system connects to a smartphone app and grid electricity supply (1 mark); considers how the rider's route, road surface and carrying requirements affect design decisions beyond the bicycle itself (1 mark); evaluates end-of-life battery disposal within the wider recycling system (1 mark). One mark per valid, contextualised point. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why user-centred design is particularly important when developing products for users with physical disabilities.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Identifies the core principle of UCD: real user needs drive every decision (1 mark); explains why assumptions are dangerous in this context: able-bodied designers will systematically underestimate grip force limitations, visual impairment constraints, and reach range reductions (1 mark); explains how UCD corrects this: repeated direct testing with disabled users reveals specific problems that specification-only design would miss (1 mark); links to a concrete outcome: e.g. adjusting handle diameter after testing with users who have arthritis produces a genuinely usable product rather than one that passes laboratory tests but fails in real use (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the Double Diamond as a design process model. Discuss both the advantages and limitations of using this model in a professional design context.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument. Advantages: provides a clear structure that avoids jumping straight to solutions (divergent thinking in Discover forces breadth); the Define phase prevents resources being spent solving the wrong problem; the second diamond's iterate-then-converge structure matches how good prototyping works; widely understood across disciplines, aiding collaborative work. Limitations: linear representation can mislead — real design is messier and often cycles back to earlier phases; the model does not specify research methods or prototyping techniques (it is a framework, not a procedure); in fast-moving commercial contexts, the full four-phase cycle may be too slow. Strong conclusion: the Double Diamond is most valuable as a shared language and structural check rather than a rigid procedure. Secure: Both sides present with some development. Developing: One side only. Emerging: Names phases but no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: A team is designing a new app-connected home heating controller. Explain how a collaborative design approach would benefit this project compared with a sequential handover approach.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks. Identifies what collaborative design involves: specialists from hardware engineering, software development, user experience design, and energy systems working together from the outset (1 mark); explains a specific benefit in this context: hardware-software interface conflicts identified early, when changes are cheap (1 mark); develops with a contextualised example: if the UI designer and hardware engineer design independently, the physical button layout may conflict with app navigation flows (1 mark); second benefit: user experience specialist ensures the controller is operable by users with limited technical knowledge from the start, not retrofitted at the end (1 mark); contrasts with sequential handover: problems found at final review are expensive to fix and may require redesign of earlier stages (1 mark); concludes: for a product where hardware and software are inseparable, collaboration is not optional (1 mark). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
On a centre lathe, which part rotates during the cutting operation?
A) The cutting tool
B) The tailstock
C) The workpiece
D) The tool post
practice_questions.marks: C) The workpiece [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two tools used when marking out a metal workpiece before cutting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: scriber / centre punch / engineer's square / vernier calliper / steel rule / engineer's blue (layout fluid) / odd-leg calliper. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how sand casting is used to produce a metal component.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• A pattern in the shape of the component is pressed into compacted sand to form a mould cavity.
• The pattern is removed and molten metal is poured into the cavity through a runner and allowed to solidify.
• The sand mould is broken apart and the casting is removed; excess metal (flash, runners) is cut away and the surface is machined if a fine finish is required. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why forging produces a stronger component than sand casting for the same shape.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Forging involves compressing a heated billet of metal between shaped dies, which deforms the metal without removing any material.
• The compressive forming process aligns the metal's grain structure along the contour of the component's shape.
• This aligned grain means the component resists the forces it will experience in service more effectively (e.g. a forged spanner's grain follows the jaw shape, resisting bending).
• In sand casting, the metal solidifies from a liquid, producing a random grain structure with no alignment; this makes castings more susceptible to fatigue and impact failure.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why die casting is preferred over sand casting for the mass production of a small zinc alloy door handle.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Die casting uses a reusable steel die; once the die is made, parts are produced very rapidly with minimal operator intervention, making it highly suited to mass production.
• Die casting produces a smooth surface finish and close dimensional tolerances, meaning little or no secondary machining is needed; this is important for a door handle that must fit pre-drilled holes precisely and look attractive.
• Zinc has a low melting point, so it can be die cast without damaging the steel die; this makes it suitable for die casting whereas ferrous metals cannot be.
• Sand casting would produce a rough surface requiring extensive finishing, would be slower per unit and would not achieve the consistent dimensional accuracy required for batch assembly.
• The high tooling cost of a die is only justified for high-volume production, so die casting is only selected over sand casting where thousands of identical parts are needed.
[6 marks — Mastering: Both processes compared on surface finish, tooling cost, volume suitability and metal type, linked to door handle context. Secure: Three factors compared with some development. Developing: Two factors, limited development. Emerging: Names processes without meaningful comparison.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using laser cutting compared to plasma cutting for shaping thin stainless steel sheet in a small workshop.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of laser cutting:
• Laser cutting produces extremely accurate, narrow kerfs and intricate profiles under CNC control; tolerances of ±0.1 mm are achievable, ideal for detailed decorative or precision components.
• Minimal heat-affected zone on thin sheet means less distortion and discolouration, important for stainless steel that is to remain unfinished.
• No physical contact with the workpiece means no clamping marks and reduced risk of surface damage.
• Laser-cut edges typically require no secondary finishing on thin sheet.
Disadvantages of laser cutting:
• High capital cost of a laser cutter; beyond the budget of many small workshops without access to a shared facility.
• Laser cutting is significantly slower than plasma when cutting thick plate (above ~6 mm); for thin sheet the speed advantage over plasma is less pronounced.
• Requires an inert assist gas (e.g. nitrogen) for stainless steel to prevent oxidation of the cut edge, adding running costs.
Advantages/disadvantages of plasma cutting in context:
• Plasma cutting is faster and cheaper for thicker material but produces a wider kerf, rougher edges and a larger heat-affected zone, requiring more secondary finishing on thin stainless.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion of both methods on accuracy, heat-affected zone, cost, speed and finishing for thin stainless in a small workshop. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed, limited development. Emerging: One-sided or superficial.]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a thermosetting polymer?
A) Polypropylene
B) High-density polyethylene
C) Urea formaldehyde
D) PVC
practice_questions.marks: C) Urea formaldehyde [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the thermoforming polymer that has a ‘living hinge’ property.
practice_questions.marks: Polypropylene (PP) [2 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between a thermoforming polymer and a thermosetting polymer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks from:
• Thermoforming polymers soften when heated and can be reshaped; thermosetting polymers cannot be re-melted once cured [1]
• Thermoforming polymers have linear/branched molecular chains; thermosetting polymers form a cross-linked 3D network on curing [1]
• Thermoforming polymers can be recycled by re-melting; thermosetting polymers cannot be recycled in the same way [1]
• Thermosetting polymers have superior heat resistance in service compared with thermoplastics [1]
(1 mark per valid contrast; max 3)

practice_questions.text: Explain why melamine formaldehyde (MF) is used to surface kitchen worktops rather than a thermoforming polymer such as polypropylene.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks from:
• MF is a thermosetting polymer with a permanently cross-linked structure [1] that gives it high surface hardness resistant to scratching from kitchen utensils [1]
• MF is resistant to heat from hot pans and boiling liquids [1] because its cross-linked structure does not soften on heating [1]
• MF is stain-resistant [1] making it easy to clean from food and drink spills [1]
• Polypropylene would soften if a hot pan was placed on it [1] because it is a thermoforming polymer with a melting point of ~160–170°C which could be approached in service [1]
(2 marks per developed point; max 4)

practice_questions.text: Explain, with reference to a specific product, the advantages of using epoxy resin rather than polyester resin as a matrix in a composite material. Include in your answer one disadvantage of epoxy resin.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names a specific high-performance application (e.g. carbon-fibre reinforced polymer aircraft component, racing bicycle frame), explains that epoxy resin produces stronger, more chemical-resistant composites than polyester resin, with lower cure shrinkage and better adhesion to reinforcement fibres. Identifies a clear disadvantage: significantly higher cost than polyester resin; longer and more complex cure times; two-part mixing required with precise ratios.
Secure: Names a product, explains one advantage of epoxy over polyester with some mechanism detail, identifies one disadvantage.
Developing: Describes epoxy resin properties without clear comparison to polyester or without product context.
Emerging: Vague reference to epoxy being ‘stronger’ without mechanism or product link.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using thermoforming polymers for food packaging, considering performance in use, manufacturing efficiency and environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed points on both sides. Advantages: thermoforming polymers (e.g. HDPE, PP) can be formed rapidly by injection moulding or blow moulding at high volume; lightweight reduces transport carbon footprint; chemically inert in contact with food; transparent grades available (PET). HDPE and PP are recyclable. Disadvantages: reliance on fossil-fuel-derived monomers; some polymer grades (PVC) raise environmental concerns at end of life; consumer recycling rates remain low in practice; some polymers absorb food odours or leach plasticisers (PVC with added plasticisers). Reaches a reasoned judgement.
Secure: Two or more developed points on each side with specific polymer examples; judgement present.
Developing: Points on both sides but limited development or lacking specific polymer names.
Emerging: Mainly one side or superficial.

practice_questions.text:
Which joint is most suitable for joining a drawer front to its side in a quality piece of furniture, resisting the repeated pulling force?
A) Butt joint
B) Dowel joint
C) Dovetail joint
D) Housing joint
practice_questions.marks: C) Dovetail joint [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two types of knock-down fitting used in flat-pack furniture construction.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: cam-lock (cam and peg / Rastex) / barrel nut and bolt / modesty block / corner block. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe why PVA adhesive is not suitable for a joint on an outdoor timber bench.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• PVA (polyvinyl acetate) is a water-based adhesive that is not waterproof, so it will absorb moisture when the bench is rained on.
• As moisture penetrates the joint, the adhesive softens and loses its bonding strength, causing the joint to creep and eventually fail.
• An exterior-grade adhesive such as epoxy resin or urea-formaldehyde should be specified instead, as these cure to a waterproof bond resistant to outdoor conditions. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a dovetail joint is chosen over a finger (box) joint for the corners of a quality handmade oak drawer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The dovetail joint's tapered interlocking tails and pins create a mechanical lock that resists the drawer being pulled out from the front; a finger joint has no such mechanical resistance and relies entirely on the adhesive.
• The dovetail joint provides a very large glue surface area (multiple faces of each tail and pin), giving an exceptionally strong permanent bond that is unlikely to fail under repeated use.
• In quality furniture, a dovetail joint is considered a mark of craftsmanship and is deliberately left visible; its appearance adds perceived value to the product.
• Oak's hardness and tight grain allows the dovetail tails and pins to be cut to a very precise fit, enhancing both the mechanical and aesthetic quality of the joint.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the factors a designer should consider when selecting a surface finish for a pine children's toy box intended for indoor use. Refer to specific finishes in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Safety: the finish must be non-toxic when dry since young children may mouth or chew the toy box; water-based acrylic paint or an EN 71-3 compliant paint should be specified rather than solvent-based oil paint.
• Durability: a children's toy box receives heavy impact and abrasion; a polyurethane varnish or hard-wearing paint finish will resist scratching better than wax or oil.
• Aesthetics: a brightly coloured opaque paint finish is typical for children's furniture and will conceal any knots or grain variation in the pine, giving a consistent appearance.
• Ease of application: water-based acrylic paint is quick-drying, low in VOCs and safer to use in a workshop or small-scale production environment than solvent-based alternatives.
• Maintenance: a painted or varnished surface can be wiped clean easily, which is a functional requirement for a toy box.
[6 marks — Mastering: Two or more factors developed with specific, named finishes and child-safety context. Secure: Two factors identified with some application to a toy box. Developing: One factor developed or points listed without context. Emerging: Vague reference to a finish without justification.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using traditional mortise-and-tenon joints compared with knock-down cam-lock fittings for the construction of a dining chair.
practice_questions.marks:
Mortise-and-tenon advantages:
• The joint's shoulders resist racking in all directions, making it the strongest traditional joint for chair frames that must resist constant lateral and torsional forces from users leaning and shifting weight.
• When glued with PVA, the large surface area of the tenon cheeks produces a very strong permanent bond that will outlast KD fittings through decades of use.
• The joint requires no metal components, keeping the chair lighter and avoiding any risk of metal corrosion in damp conditions.
• From a quality and craft perspective, a well-cut mortise-and-tenon joint adds to the perceived value of the product and is expected in quality hand-made furniture.
Mortise-and-tenon disadvantages:
• Cutting and fitting the joint requires skilled labour and time; each joint must be individually fitted, making it expensive to produce at scale.
• Once glued, the chair cannot be disassembled for flat-pack shipping without destroying the joint.
KD cam-lock advantages:
• Cam-lock fittings allow the chair to be supplied flat-packed for efficient, low-cost shipping and assembled by the customer without tools.
• Components can be replaced individually if damaged, extending the product's life.
KD cam-lock disadvantages:
• Cam-lock fittings provide little resistance to racking compared with a mortise-and-tenon joint; over time, repeated loading loosens the fitting and the chair becomes unstable.
• Exposed fittings require recesses accurately drilled in both panels; alignment errors during manufacture cause visible gaps at the joint face.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages per method, applied to a dining chair. Secure: Two of each with some development. Developing: Limited development or imbalanced. Emerging: Superficial or one-sided.]

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of drawing that shows a product from three views — front, side, and plan — drawn to scale with exact dimensions.
practice_questions.marks: Orthographic projection [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between an isometric drawing and a perspective drawing.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for two of: isometric uses no vanishing point / perspective uses one or two vanishing points (1 mark); isometric draws all edges to true length / perspective lines recede to the horizon (1 mark); isometric keeps parallel lines parallel / perspective lines converge (1 mark); isometric can give accurate proportions for manufacture / perspective gives the impression of depth as seen by the eye (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how an exploded diagram is used to communicate assembly information for a flat-pack product.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Components are shown separated along a central axis (1 mark); the spatial relationship between parts reveals their assembly sequence (1 mark); the diagram communicates the order of assembly and how parts fit together without requiring written language (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer might use a physical model at an early stage rather than a fully rendered CAD drawing when presenting to a client.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Physical model allows the client to handle and assess the product's form and proportions in three dimensions (1 mark); reveals ergonomic issues (such as whether a handle fits the hand comfortably) that a 2D or digital view cannot communicate (1 mark); clients without technical drawing literacy can evaluate a physical model without needing training (1 mark); early-stage models are made quickly from card or foam, making them cheap to modify if the client requests changes (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of CAD software compared with traditional hand drawing when communicating design ideas to a manufacturer. Discuss both advantages and disadvantages of CAD.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced, developed argument. Advantages of CAD: dimensions are precise and consistent (no transcription errors); models can be modified instantly when specifications change; CAD files can be exported directly to CAM machinery, eliminating re-drawing; simulation tools (FEA, fluid dynamics) allow failure modes to be eliminated before physical production; 3D models can be shared globally in seconds. Disadvantages: requires specialist software licences and trained operators; early-stage ideation is slower in CAD than freehand sketching; complex organic forms can be difficult to model without high-end surfacing tools; overreliance on CAD can reduce a designer's ability to think and communicate spatially without a screen. Conclusion: CAD is superior for manufacturing communication and simulation but does not replace freehand sketching in early ideation. Secure: Both sides with some development. Developing: One side only. Emerging: General points only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: A designer is producing an assembly manual for a new flat-pack garden chair. Explain the most suitable communication techniques for two different sections of the manual: the component identification section and the assembly sequence section.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per section). Component identification: annotated isometric or perspective drawing showing each part named and numbered (1 mark); isometric is appropriate because it shows true proportions of all parts clearly without visual distortion (1 mark); annotations identify part names, quantities, and materials so the user can check all components are present (1 mark). Assembly sequence: exploded diagram with numbered steps (1 mark); components shown separated along the assembly axis reveal the order of fitting without requiring written language (1 mark); exploded diagrams work across language barriers and for users with limited reading ability (1 mark). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which printing process uses flexible polymer relief plates and is the dominant method for printing onto corrugated board?
A) Offset lithography
B) Screen printing
C) Flexography
D) Digital inkjet
practice_questions.marks: C) Flexography [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the four ink colours used in full-colour offset lithographic printing.
practice_questions.marks: All four required for 2 marks: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Key (Black). Accept CMYK as the abbreviation if the full names or colours are given alongside. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how UV spot varnish is applied to a printed board surface and explain its effect.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
- UV spot varnish is applied selectively over specific design elements (e.g. a logo or image) using a printing plate or digital print engine.
- The varnish is cured instantly by exposure to ultraviolet light, hardening to a high-gloss, slightly raised surface.
- The contrast between the glossy spot-varnished area and the surrounding matt or satin surface draws the eye and adds a tactile quality that communicates premium value. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a packaging designer would specify digital inkjet printing rather than offset lithography for a run of 200 personalised gift boxes.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Digital inkjet requires no printing plates, so there is no plate-making set-up cost regardless of how many designs are printed.
- Each box can carry a different name or image (variable data printing) without any additional cost or changeover time, which is essential for personalised gifting.
- At 200 units, the set-up cost of making four lithographic plates would make the per-unit cost very high, far exceeding the cost of digital printing.
- Lithography is only economical at volumes of several thousand sheets, where the fixed plate cost is spread over a large number of units. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the differences between gloss lamination and UV spot varnish as surface finishing techniques, including why each is applied and the effect each produces on a printed carton.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Gloss lamination bonds a transparent BOPP film across the entire printed surface (flood application), making it waterproof, scuff-resistant and increasing board stiffness.
- UV spot varnish is applied selectively to specific areas of the printed design, creating a high-gloss, slightly raised tactile contrast against the surrounding surface.
- Lamination is primarily functional: it protects the surface from moisture, abrasion and handling, making it suitable for products that experience heavy use (menus, carrier bags, brochure covers).
- UV spot varnish is primarily aesthetic: it creates a premium visual and tactile quality by highlighting key design elements such as logos or product images.
- Lamination adds more measurable protection but makes the board harder to recycle; UV spot varnish adds less protection but is thinner and less of a recycling barrier.
[6 marks - Mastering: Both processes fully described and contrasted in terms of application method, purpose and carton context. Secure: Both described with some contrast; purpose linked but not fully developed. Developing: One process well described; second superficial. Emerging: Vague reference to one process only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using offset lithography compared with screen printing for producing 50,000 units of printed retail packaging.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of offset lithography:
- Produces the highest quality photographic image reproduction via CMYK halftone dot printing, suitable for detailed product photography on packaging.
- At 50,000 units, the fixed cost of making four printing plates is easily amortised across the run, giving a very low cost per sheet.
- High-speed rotary presses can print thousands of sheets per hour, meeting a tight production schedule.
- Consistent, repeatable colour across the entire run is maintained by ink density controls, important for brand colour accuracy.
Disadvantages of offset lithography:
- Four plates must be made for a full-colour job, adding a significant set-up cost that makes it uneconomical for short runs.
- Lithography works best on flat sheets of paper and board; it cannot easily print onto corrugated or three-dimensional substrates.
- Any design change (e.g. a regulatory update on food packaging) requires a new plate, adding cost and delay.
Advantages of screen printing at 50,000 units:
- Screen printing deposits a thick, opaque ink layer that can print on dark or textured boards where lithography would produce dull, washed-out colours.
- Specialist inks (metallic, UV-reactive, tactile) can be used in screen printing that are not compatible with lithographic presses.
Disadvantages:
- Screen printing is significantly slower than lithography and more expensive per unit at high volumes, making 50,000 units costly.
- Each colour requires a separate screen set-up, and fine photographic detail is harder to achieve than with lithographic halftone dots.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced comparison with at least two developed points for each process, linked to the 50,000-unit context. Secure: Two points per process with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

practice_questions.text:
Which printing method works exclusively on white polyester fabric by converting ink into gas under heat?
A) Block printing
B) Screen printing
C) Digital inkjet printing
D) Sublimation printing
practice_questions.marks: D) Sublimation printing [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two functional finishes that can be applied to fabrics and state one product each is used on.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per correct finish + product pairing. Accept any two of: waterproofing/DWR — outdoor jacket/tent; flame-retardant — children's nightwear/furniture; stain-resistant — school tie/table linen; crease-resistant — cotton shirt; brushing/raising — flannelette/fleece. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a flat-bed screen printing process is set up for a two-colour fabric design.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• A separate screen is made for each colour: the mesh is coated with light-sensitive emulsion and a photographic positive of one colour's design is exposed onto it; unexposed emulsion washes away to leave open mesh areas.
• Two screens (one per colour) are aligned in sequence over the fabric; dye paste is forced through the open mesh onto the fabric for each colour separately.
• The fabric passes to each screen in turn; the alignment (registration) of the screens must be precise so the two colours line up correctly. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how Gore-Tex achieves both waterproofing and breathability, and why both properties are important for a hiking jacket.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Gore-Tex consists of a microporous polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) membrane laminated to the outer fabric; the membrane contains billions of microscopic pores per square centimetre.
• The pores are small enough to block liquid water droplets from penetrating inwards (waterproofing), preventing rain from soaking the wearer.
• The pores are large enough to allow water vapour molecules (sweat) to escape outwards (breathability), preventing the jacket from becoming uncomfortable and clammy during exertion.
• For a hiker, both properties together are essential: waterproofing prevents hypothermia from wet conditions; breathability prevents overheating and moisture build-up from exercise.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the differences between screen printing and digital printing for a textile manufacturer, and evaluate which method is more suitable for a print run of 50 personalised team football shirts.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Screen printing has a high set-up cost (one screen made per colour, each requiring exposure and preparation), but once set up the cost per unit is very low — making it efficient for large runs of identical items.
• Digital printing requires no screens or set-up cost; the design is sent directly from a computer to the printer. Cost per unit is higher than screen printing for large runs but low for short runs.
• Digital printing can reproduce unlimited colours and photographic images in one pass; screen printing is limited by the number of screens (each additional colour adds cost).
• For 50 personalised football shirts (each with a different player name or number): digital printing is clearly more suitable because there is no set-up cost, each design can be unique, and the short run (50 units) would not justify the screen-making cost.
• A screen-printing set-up for 50 shirts with individual names would require a different screen for every name, making it extremely expensive and impractical.
[6 marks — Mastering: Both methods fully compared and final recommendation clearly justified with reference to run length, personalisation and cost. Secure: Both methods compared, recommendation made with partial justification. Developing: One method described; superficial comparison. Emerging: Vague or one method only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of incorporating smart textile technology (such as conductive yarns or thermochromic dyes) into a range of children's school uniform.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
• Thermochromic dyes could be used to create an engaging colour-change element in school ties or badges — stimulating children's interest and giving the uniform a distinctive identity.
• Conductive yarns could integrate an NFC chip or RFID tag into the garment to replace ID cards for school gate entry or library loans, simplifying administration and reducing lost cards.
• A thermochromic temperature indicator could alert staff to a child with a dangerously elevated or lowered body temperature — useful in sports changing rooms or for children with medical conditions.
Disadvantages:
• Smart textiles add significantly to manufacturing cost, making the uniform less affordable for families — a major concern for schools serving disadvantaged communities.
• Electronic components in school uniform must withstand vigorous washing, playground activity and accidental damage; durability in everyday school wear has not been proven at scale.
• Thermochromic dyes and their chemical treatments must pass strict safety tests for children's clothing — formaldehyde-free and skin-safe — adding regulatory complexity and cost.
• Data privacy concerns arise if RFID or biometric garments track children's movements; school governors and parents may object on safeguarding grounds.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion, at least two developed points per side, all linked convincingly to the school uniform context. Secure: Two points per side with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development or imbalanced. Emerging: Superficial or one-sided.]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a thermo-chromic material?
A) It returns to a pre-set shape when heated above its transition temperature
B) It changes colour reversibly in response to a change in temperature
C) It becomes electrically conductive when compressed
D) It emits light when an electrical current passes through it
practice_questions.marks: B) It changes colour reversibly in response to a change in temperature [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the stimulus and response for a quantum tunnelling composite (QTC).
practice_questions.marks:
• Stimulus: compression / pressure applied to the material [1 mark]
• Response: changes from an electrical insulator to a conductor [1 mark]
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how shape memory alloy (SMA) behaves when cooled and then heated, and name one application.
practice_questions.marks:
• When cooled (below transition temperature), SMA can be deformed into a new shape (1).
• When heated above its transition temperature, it returns to its pre-set original shape (1).
• Application: medical stent inserted compressed and expands with body heat / self-straightening eyeglass frames / thermostatic valve [any one] (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why polymorph is useful for creating custom-fit product components. Refer to its material properties in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per developed point:
• Polymorph becomes mouldable at approximately 62°C (in warm water) (1), allowing a designer or user to shape it by hand to exactly the required form without specialist tools (1).
• When cooled to room temperature it becomes rigid and holds its shape (1), making it suitable for structural components such as grips or supports that need to resist deformation in use (1).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A designer is developing a children's spoon that warns parents when food is too hot. Explain, with reference to a smart material, how the spoon could be designed to perform this function without electronic components.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies thermo-chromic material specifically, explains the stimulus (temperature above a set threshold) and the response (colour change), applies this to the spoon context (e.g. handle changes from green to red when food exceeds 40°C), considers safety and reversibility. Appropriate material fully integrated into product function.
Secure: Thermo-chromic correctly identified with stimulus and response explained; spoon context embedded in at least one point.
Developing: Smart material identified but response or stimulus vague; product context limited.
Emerging: General reference to changing colour; no specific material named or mechanism explained.
[6 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using shape memory alloy (SMA) in a medical stent compared with a traditional mechanical expanding stent.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of SMA advantages (no mechanical inflation needed, simpler insertion, responds to body temperature automatically, lightweight, biocompatible nitinol) and disadvantages (precise transition temperature required, cost, potential for incomplete expansion, limited to applications within the temperature range). Traditional stent comparison embedded. Weighted judgement about which is more suitable in which circumstances.
Secure: Two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages; some specific detail (e.g. body temperature, nitinol, biocompatibility); conclusion present.
Developing: Points made but imbalanced or underdeveloped; limited specific material knowledge.
Emerging: Simple list of pros/cons; no medical or material specifics.
[8 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text:
Which adhesive would be most suitable for joining two pieces of acrylic to make a display box?
A) PVA woodworking adhesive
B) Tensol solvent cement
C) Contact adhesive
D) Hot-melt glue
practice_questions.marks: B) Tensol solvent cement [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two advantages of using a snap fit rather than a screw to join two polymer components.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per advantage up to 2. Accept: no additional parts/fixings needed; faster assembly (no tool required); lower production cost per unit; can be designed for one-handed operation; reduces part count and assembly time. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe why polypropylene (PP) is particularly well suited for use in snap-fit joints.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• PP has excellent fatigue resistance, meaning it can flex repeatedly without fracturing at the root of the snap-fit cantilever.
• PP is a thermoforming polymer that can be accurately injection moulded to the tight dimensional tolerances required for a reliable snap-fit engagement force.
• PP is lightweight and food-safe, making it appropriate for the food containers and medical devices where snap fits are commonly used. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why Tensol solvent cement cannot be used to join a phenol formaldehyde (Bakelite) component.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Tensol is a solvent cement that works by dissolving the surface of the polymer, allowing the chains of two pieces to intermingle and bond as the solvent evaporates.
• Phenol formaldehyde is a thermosetting polymer with permanent cross-links between its polymer chains.
• The cross-linked structure makes thermosets highly chemically resistant — the solvent in Tensol cannot dissolve or penetrate the surface.
• A more appropriate adhesive would be a two-part epoxy such as Araldite, which bonds through a chemical cross-linking reaction rather than surface dissolution. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the term 'self-finishing' as applied to polymers and explain the economic and environmental advantages this provides in high-volume manufacture.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Definition: self-finishing means the surface produced by the moulding or extrusion process is the final surface — no secondary painting, varnishing or plating is required, because pigments are incorporated throughout the material during manufacture.
Economic: eliminates the capital cost of a spray booth or plating line; removes paint/coating material cost; reduces labour for a secondary finishing stage; speeds up production throughput.
Environmental: avoids VOC (volatile organic compound) emissions from solvent-based paints; reduces energy used in drying/curing ovens; eliminates paint waste and associated disposal costs.
Example: an ABS computer mouse shell emerges from the injection mould in its final colour with its surface texture already formed by the polished steel mould — it proceeds directly to assembly.
[6 marks — Mastering: self-finishing defined accurately with both economic and environmental advantages developed with examples. Secure: defined with two advantages covered but limited examples. Developing: definition correct but only one advantage developed. Emerging: vague reference to polymers not needing painting with no explanation of why or what the benefit is.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of plastic welding compared with using adhesives to join polymer components.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of plastic welding: creates a molecular-level fusion — the joint is part of the material itself, often as strong as the parent material; produces leak-tight joints (PVC pipes, fuel tanks); no chemicals introduced into the joint that might degrade over time; ultrasonic welding is fast and suitable for high-volume automation.
Disadvantages of plastic welding: only works on thermoforming polymers — thermosets cannot be welded; requires specialist equipment (hot gas welder, ultrasonic welder); skill-dependent for consistent quality on manual hot gas welding; the joint is permanent and cannot be disassembled.
Advantages of adhesives: epoxy bonds dissimilar materials including thermosets; Tensol is low-cost and accessible; minimal equipment needed for small-scale production.
Disadvantages of adhesives: Tensol limited to compatible thermoforming pairs; epoxy requires accurate mixing and has cure time; adhesive layer may degrade in UV or solvent environments; joint faces must be clean and flat.
[8 marks — Mastering: sustained balanced discussion, at least two developed points per side, specific welding methods (ultrasonic/hot gas) and adhesive types (Tensol/epoxy) named, economic and technical factors both considered. Secure: two points per side with development. Developing: limited development, unbalanced. Emerging: one-sided or very superficial.]

practice_questions.text:
Which welding process uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode and is best suited to thin stainless steel sheet?
A) MIG welding
B) TIG welding
C) Arc (MMA) welding
D) Brazing
practice_questions.marks: B) TIG welding [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two methods of providing corrosion protection to a mild steel garden gate.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: painting / powder coating / galvanising / electroplating (zinc) / dip coating / primer application. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how galvanising protects steel from corrosion.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• The steel is dipped into a bath of molten zinc, which coats the surface with a layer of zinc.
• The zinc provides a physical barrier preventing moisture and oxygen reaching the steel surface.
• If the coating is scratched, the zinc acts as a sacrificial anode and corrodes preferentially, continuing to protect the exposed steel beneath because zinc is more reactive than iron. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the differences between welding, brazing and soldering as methods of permanently joining metals.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In welding, the base metals are heated to their melting point and fuse together with a filler of the same composition; the joint becomes part of the parent material and is as strong as or stronger than the base metal.
• In brazing, the base metal does not melt; a brass or silver-based filler alloy with a melting point above 450°C is melted by a torch and flows into the joint by capillary action.
• In soldering, the base metal again does not melt; a tin-based filler with a melting point below 450°C is used; the joint is weaker than a brazed or welded joint.
• Soldering is therefore used where heat input must be minimised (e.g. electronic circuit boards) and structural strength is not the priority.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why powder coating is preferred over liquid paint for the finish on a steel bicycle frame intended for year-round outdoor use.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Powder coating is applied as a dry electrostatic powder and cured at 180-200°C, producing a chemically cross-linked polymer film that bonds strongly to the metal surface.
• The resulting coating is significantly harder and more impact-resistant than conventional liquid paint, which is important for a bicycle frame exposed to stone chips and knocks.
• Powder coating provides a more uniform film thickness with no runs or drips, improving the visual quality and consistency of the finish.
• It is more resistant to chipping and scratching, meaning the steel is less likely to be exposed to moisture and therefore less likely to corrode at damage points.
• Powder coating produces very low VOC (volatile organic compound) emissions compared to solvent-based paints, making it more environmentally responsible.
• For liquid paint to perform comparably, multiple priming and topcoat layers would be needed, increasing production time and cost; powder coating achieves a superior result in a single cure step.
[6 marks — Mastering: At least three specific advantages of powder coating linked to the bicycle-frame context with reference to corrosion, mechanical properties and process efficiency. Secure: Two advantages with some development. Developing: One advantage; limited development or context. Emerging: Vague preference stated without explanation.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using MIG welding compared to riveting for permanently joining mild steel panels in the manufacture of a car body.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of MIG welding:
• MIG welding fuses the base metal together, producing a continuous joint that is as strong as the parent material; this is important for crash safety and structural integrity.
• Automated MIG welding robots operate at very high speed on a production line, reducing cycle time and labour cost per vehicle.
• Welded joints create a smooth, flush surface that is ideal for applying primer and paint without the raised heads associated with rivets.
• No holes need to be drilled through the panels prior to joining, reducing the risk of stress concentrations at hole edges.
Disadvantages of MIG welding:
• The heat introduced during welding can cause distortion and warping of thin sheet panels, requiring subsequent straightening operations.
• Welded joints are permanent; if a panel needs replacement after a minor collision, the weld must be cut away, increasing repair cost and time.
• MIG welding of coated or galvanised steel may produce toxic fumes from the zinc coating, requiring extraction and PPE.
• Riveting by comparison is fast to set up for low volume, requires no heat, can join dissimilar metals and is easily disassembled; however, rivet heads are visible and the joint is weaker in tension than an equivalent weld.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion of at least two developed advantages and two disadvantages of MIG welding relative to riveting, linked to car body manufacturing context (strength, speed, surface finish, repairability). Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or superficial.]

before.exam_tip_html: For any question comparing welding, brazing and soldering, the examiner is looking for you to identify: (1) whether the base metal melts, (2) the filler material and its melting point range, and (3) the resulting joint strength or application. A Mastering-level answer for a 6-mark question would also include a specific product example for each process and comment on the skill or equipment required. Do not just say a joint is “stronger” — explain why (e.g. “welding fuses the base metal, making the joint continuous with the parent material, whereas soldering only adheres a low-melting-point filler to the surface”).

practice_questions.text:
A lever has its fulcrum 0.1 m from the load and 0.5 m from the effort. What is the mechanical advantage of this lever?
A) 0.2
B) 2
C) 5
D) 50
State the formula used to calculate the gear ratio of a pair of meshing gears.
practice_questions.marks: Gear ratio = number of teeth on driven gear ÷ number of teeth on driver gear. [2 marks: 1 for identifying driven/driver correctly, 1 for correct ratio structure]

practice_questions.text: A driver gear with 20 teeth meshes with a driven gear with 60 teeth. The driver rotates at 300 rpm. Calculate the gear ratio and the output speed of the driven gear. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Gear ratio = 60 ÷ 20 = 3:1 [1 mark for correct ratio]
Output speed = 300 ÷ 3 = 100 rpm [1 mark for correct calculation, 1 mark for units (rpm)] [3 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A lever is balanced on a fulcrum. A 90 N load is placed 0.2 m from the fulcrum. Calculate the effort required at a point 0.6 m from the fulcrum on the other side to keep the lever in equilibrium. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Principle of moments: Effort × 0.6 = 90 × 0.2 [1 mark for correct equation setup]
Effort × 0.6 = 18
Effort = 18 ÷ 0.6 = 30 N [1 mark for correct calculation, 1 mark for units (N)] [3 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A belt-and-pulley system has a driver pulley of 40 mm diameter and a driven pulley of 160 mm diameter. The driver runs at 800 rpm. Calculate the velocity ratio and the output speed of the driven pulley. Explain what happens to the torque as a result of this ratio.
practice_questions.marks:
VR = 160 ÷ 40 = 4 [1 mark]
Output speed = 800 ÷ 4 = 200 rpm [1 mark for calculation, 1 mark for units]
Torque increases by a factor of 4 at the output [1 mark]
Explanation: a larger driven pulley turns more slowly but provides greater turning force [1 mark]
Application: this principle is used in washing machine drum drives where high torque is needed to agitate heavy wet laundry at low drum speed [1 mark]
[6 marks — Mastering: All calculation steps correct, torque effect explained with product context. Secure: Calculation correct, torque direction stated without full explanation. Developing: VR correct but output speed or torque explanation incomplete. Emerging: Formula stated but substitution or calculation incorrect.]

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating a manual can opener. The turning handle has an effort arm of 80 mm from the pivot and the cutting blade is attached 20 mm from the pivot. Calculate the mechanical advantage. Evaluate whether this design is suitable for a person with reduced grip strength and suggest one specific modification to improve it.
practice_questions.marks:
Calculation:
MA = 80 ÷ 20 = 4 [2 marks: 1 formula, 1 correct answer]
Evaluation:
• MA of 4 means the user applies four times less force than the cutting force, which reduces the effort needed — suitable for most users but may still require significant grip strength. [2 marks]
• A person with reduced grip strength may still struggle if the friction from the can rim or dull blade adds resistance not captured in the MA calculation alone. [2 marks]
• The handle diameter and texture also affect comfort — a thin hard handle concentrates force on the palm, increasing discomfort. [1 mark]
Modification:
• Increase the effort arm to, e.g., 160 mm — doubling it to give MA = 8, halving the required effort. [1 mark]
• OR fit a soft ergonomic grip to spread contact force across a wider palm area. [1 mark]
• OR add a ratchet mechanism so continuous rotation is not required, reducing peak grip force. [1 mark]
[8 marks — Mastering: Correct calculation, sustained evaluation addressing suitability and limitations with quantified evidence, specific justified modification. Secure: Correct calculation, basic suitability evaluation, modification stated. Developing: Partial calculation or evaluation without modification. Emerging: Attempt at calculation only.]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a low-fidelity prototype?
A) A near-production model made from the correct materials used in final approval testing
B) A rough model made quickly from card or foam to test the form or scale of a product
C) A computer simulation that predicts stress distribution under load
D) A digital animation of the final product for client presentation
practice_questions.marks: B) A rough model made quickly from card or foam to test the form or scale of a product [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'ergonomics' in product design.
