practice_questions.marks: Ergonomics is the science of designing products to fit the physical and cognitive abilities of users (1 mark), minimising discomfort, fatigue, and error during use (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a designer would use anthropometric data when designing the seat height of a children's chair for primary school classrooms.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Identifies the relevant body measurement: seated popliteal height (distance from the floor to the back of the bent knee) for the target age range (1 mark); explains percentile application: uses 5th to 95th percentile data to ensure the chair height works for 90% of the target user group (1 mark); explains the practical outcome: sets a seat height range that allows feet to rest flat on the floor without the seat edge cutting into the thigh, supporting circulation and posture (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is important for designers to use iterative testing throughout the design process rather than only testing the final prototype.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Early testing reveals structural or ergonomic problems when changes are cheap (1 mark); testing a low-fidelity prototype can identify a specification error before expensive materials are committed (1 mark); feedback at each stage informs subsequent design decisions, not just product polish (1 mark); a design error discovered only at the final prototype stage may require the entire design to be reworked, whereas the same error found early may be resolved by a minor specification change (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A designer is developing a new electric power drill for professional tradespeople. Evaluate how the designer could use user testing to assess and improve the ergonomics of the drill's handle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates the testing process at multiple stages. Initial low-fidelity handle tests using foam models allow a range of grip spans and diameters to be assessed quickly; anthropometric data (5th to 95th percentile grip span for adult workers) informs the starting dimensions. Structured user testing with professional tradespeople involves task-based tests under realistic loads and durations, revealing fatigue onset and pain points that brief handling cannot detect. Think-aloud protocol captures cognitive ergonomics: unclear trigger mechanisms or awkward mode-switching positions are identified. Rating scales quantify comfort, control, and perceived safety. Findings inform iterative specification changes: reducing handle diameter, adding grip zones, adjusting trigger force. Final high-fidelity prototype confirms changes work before production tooling. Strong evaluation acknowledges limitations: user testing a small panel may not capture all hand sizes or use cases across the professional trades. Secure: Testing process described at two or more stages with clear link to improvement. Developing: Testing described but links to specific ergonomic decisions are weak. Emerging: General description of user testing only. [10 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what designers mean by 'fitness for purpose' and describe two tests a designer might carry out to evaluate whether a children's waterproof lunchbox meets this criterion.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks. Fitness for purpose definition: the product successfully fulfils the requirements of the design brief and meets all criteria in the design specification (1 mark); for this product, this means the lunchbox keeps food contained, remains waterproof, is safe for children to use, and withstands everyday handling (1 mark). Test 1: water immersion test — submerge the lunchbox in water for a specified period (e.g. 10 minutes) and check for moisture ingress inside; this directly tests the waterproof seal performance against a measurable design criterion (1 mark + application 1 mark). Test 2: drop test — drop the lunchbox from a height representing a typical child dropping it (e.g. 1 m onto a hard floor) and inspect the seal, hinges and body for damage; this tests whether the product survives realistic handling conditions (1 mark + application 1 mark). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
What recycling code number is assigned to PET (polyethylene terephthalate)?
A) 2
B) 3
C) 1
D) 5
practice_questions.marks: C) 1 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why thermosetting polymers do not carry a recycling code.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per reason up to 2. Accept: they cannot be remelted (permanent cross-links); they cannot be sorted into a melt-reprocess recycling stream; applying heat causes them to char rather than soften; there is no established commercial recycling process for them. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between batch production and mass production when manufacturing polymer products.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• In batch production, a set quantity of identical products is made before the production line is reconfigured for a different product or variant; tooling costs are moderate.
• In mass production, the same product is manufactured continuously at very high volume; processes such as injection moulding and extrusion run at high speed with high tooling investment but very low unit cost.
• Mass production typically requires expensive automated tooling such as multi-cavity injection moulds; batch production may use lower-cost tools such as vacuum forming moulds made from MDF or cast aluminium. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what microplastics are and why they present a significant environmental concern.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Microplastics are plastic fragments smaller than 5 mm produced when larger plastic items break down under UV light and mechanical abrasion.
• They cannot be captured by standard water treatment systems and enter rivers, oceans and soil.
• Marine organisms ingest microplastics, which enter the food chain and accumulate in fish tissue that humans consume.
• Microplastics have been detected in human blood, lung tissue and placentas; their full health implications are still under investigation but raise serious concerns. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer could apply three of the 6 Rs when designing a reusable HDPE food storage container to improve its sustainability.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reduce: optimise wall thickness using finite element analysis to minimise HDPE material while maintaining structural performance, reducing crude-oil consumption and transport weight per unit.
Reuse: design the container for multiple fill-and-wash cycles by specifying HDPE's food-safe, dishwasher-resistant properties rather than single-use LDPE film; add a reliable PP snap-fit lid to avoid use-and-discard behaviour.
Recycle: mark the container with code 2 (HDPE) using a moulded-in symbol; design the base to be flat and uniform so it stacks and sorts easily in recycling facilities; avoid bonded multi-material labels that contaminate the HDPE stream.
[6 marks — Mastering: three Rs each fully developed with HDPE-specific detail and a real design decision linked to each principle. Secure: three Rs identified and developed with some material-specific content. Developing: two or three Rs named with limited development. Emerging: general sustainability comments without naming or applying the Rs framework.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using thermoforming polymers rather than thermosetting polymers in the context of sustainability and end-of-life disposal.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of thermoforming polymers: carry recycling codes 1–7 enabling consumer sorting; can be remelted and reprocessed into new products, reducing demand for virgin crude oil; recycled PP and HDPE are used in furniture, drainage pipes and automotive parts; lightweight; can incorporate recycled content.
Disadvantages of thermoforming polymers: each recycling cycle degrades molecular weight — recycled PET cannot be used for food-contact bottles without blending virgin material; microplastic pollution risk from single-use forms such as LDPE bags and EPS; not all codes are kerbside-collected; contamination causes batch rejection; do not biodegrade.
Advantages of thermosetting polymers: inherently more durable and longer-lasting in service (melamine worktops, Bakelite switches) — longer product life reduces replacement frequency; do not microplastic-degrade in the environment under normal conditions.
Disadvantages of thermosetting polymers: no established recycling route; permanent cross-links mean end-of-life is landfill or incineration; incineration releases CO₂ and potentially toxic by-products; cannot be repaired by remelting; chemical recycling (pyrolysis) remains expensive and energy-intensive.
[8 marks — Mastering: sustained balanced discussion with at least two developed points per side, specific polymer examples throughout, and acknowledgement of nuance such as degradation in recycling cycles or the durability advantage of thermosets. Secure: two points per side with some development. Developing: limited development, unbalanced. Emerging: one-sided or very superficial.]

practice_questions.text:
A bicycle chain is pulled tight between the pedal gear and the rear wheel gear while the cyclist pedals. What type of stress is the chain experiencing?
A) Compression
B) Torsion
C) Tension
D) Shear
practice_questions.marks: C) Tension [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the type of stress acting on the top surface of a wooden shelf that sags under the weight of heavy books.
practice_questions.marks: Compression. [1 mark] (The top of a bent beam/shelf is in compression; the bottom is in tension. Accept 'bending' as the overall stress type with 'compression at the top surface' for full credit.)

practice_questions.text: Describe how corrugating a sheet of card increases its resistance to bending.
practice_questions.marks:
• The corrugated layer creates a wavy internal structure with peaks and troughs. [1 mark]
• The vertical elements of the corrugation resist compressive forces acting from above. [1 mark]
• This increases the card's stiffness under bending loads without significantly increasing the material mass. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain why an I-beam profile resists bending forces more efficiently than a solid rectangular section of the same mass of steel.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• When a beam bends, stress is highest at the top (compression) and bottom (tension) surfaces and nearly zero at the neutral axis in the centre. [1 mark]
• An I-beam concentrates its material in the flanges at the top and bottom, where bending stress is highest. [1 mark]
• The thin web in the middle carries little of the bending load, so placing material there (as a solid section does) is structurally inefficient. [1 mark]
• The same mass of steel in an I-section therefore provides far greater bending resistance than a solid rectangular section. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating a rigid shoulder bag from a woven cotton fabric. Explain, with reference to specific reinforcement techniques, how the structural integrity of the bag can be improved so that it withstands tension in the strap and prevents the base from deforming under load.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Nylon or polypropylene webbing should be used for the shoulder strap because webbing has very high tensile strength along its length and will resist the tension created by the weight of the bag's contents. [2 marks]
• Interfacing bonded to the base panel adds rigidity, distributing the compressive and bending forces from the loaded bag contents over a wider area rather than allowing the fabric to deform. [2 marks]
• Reinforced stitching at stress concentration points — where the strap attaches to the bag body — distributes shear forces that would otherwise cause the strap to tear out. [1 mark]
• An internal base board or rigid panel can be inserted to resist the shear and bending loads at the base. [1 mark]
[6 marks — Mastering: Three techniques named with material-specific justification linked to the specific stress type each resists. Secure: Two techniques with justification. Developing: One technique named with basic explanation. Emerging: Vague suggestion ('make it stronger') without technique or stress type.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using glass-reinforced polymer (GRP) compared to sheet aluminium for the bodywork panels of a sports car.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of GRP over sheet aluminium:
• GRP can be formed into complex double-curvature shapes (such as curved body panels) without the expensive tooling and pressing equipment required to shape aluminium.
• GRP has a lower density than aluminium (approximately 1.8 g/cm³ vs 2.7 g/cm³), reducing the vehicle's overall mass and improving performance.
• GRP does not corrode, reducing maintenance requirements and extending panel life in wet climates.
• GRP panels can be repaired with filler and resin without specialist equipment; dented aluminium panels often require panel beating and repainting.
Disadvantages of GRP:
• GRP has lower stiffness than aluminium for the same thickness; panels may flex or vibrate at high speed unless additional thickness or ribbing is added.
• GRP is more difficult to recycle at end of life; thermoset resins cannot be remelted, whereas aluminium is highly recyclable.
• GRP is more flammable than aluminium and may release toxic fumes if the vehicle catches fire.
• Surface finish on GRP requires gel-coat application and careful mould preparation; aluminium can be anodised or painted directly.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages specific to sports car bodywork. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development, limited balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

practice_questions.text:
Which scale of production is most appropriate for manufacturing 2 million aluminium drink cans per day?
A) One-off production
B) Batch production
C) Mass production
D) Prototype production
practice_questions.marks: C) Mass production [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the most commercially important shape memory alloy and state its two constituent elements.
practice_questions.marks: Nitinol [1 mark]; nickel and titanium [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe why recycling aluminium is significantly more sustainable than producing virgin aluminium from bauxite.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Recycling aluminium uses only approximately 5% of the energy required to smelt primary aluminium from bauxite ore.
• This greatly reduces CO₂ emissions associated with aluminium production, lowering its carbon footprint.
• Recycling also reduces the need for bauxite mining, which destroys habitats, pollutes waterways and generates significant quantities of toxic red mud waste as a by-product. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a nitinol stent is used to treat a blocked coronary artery.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Nitinol is a shape memory alloy with a transformation temperature set close to body temperature (37°C).
• The stent is cooled below its transformation temperature and compressed (crimped) onto a catheter so it takes up a small diameter, allowing it to be guided through the blood vessel.
• Once positioned inside the blocked artery, the stent is exposed to body temperature and recovers its pre-set expanded shape, opening the artery and holding it open.
• This approach eliminates the need for a mechanical inflation device (balloon), reducing the complexity of the procedure and the risk of damage to the artery wall.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how applying the 6Rs framework to a steel garden gate can reduce its environmental impact across its full lifecycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reduce: design the gate using less steel (e.g. hollow tube section rather than solid bar) to reduce embodied energy without compromising structural performance.
Reuse: if the gate is removed during renovation, it can be sold or donated for reuse at another property, avoiding the energy cost of remanufacture.
Recycle: at end of life, the steel can be 100% recycled; recycled steel uses approximately 74% less energy than virgin steel, significantly reducing lifecycle carbon.
Refuse: reject an over-specified design or an unnecessary part; for example, refuse decorative cast panels that add steel and weight for no functional gain.
Repair: rather than replacing a corroded gate, sandblasting and re-painting or re-galvanising extends its life, deferring replacement and the associated resource consumption.
Rethink: designing the gate without mixed-material components (e.g. plastic decorative elements bonded to steel) makes end-of-life recycling easier and more effective.
[6 marks — Mastering: At least four of the 6Rs applied specifically to the steel gate with developed environmental impact explanation. Secure: Three Rs applied with some development. Developing: Two Rs listed with limited development; little link to environmental impact. Emerging: Vague mention of recycling without development.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using batch production compared to mass production for manufacturing cast iron garden furniture.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of batch production for cast iron garden furniture:
• Lower initial capital investment; sand casting equipment and tooling is cheaper than the automated lines and dies required for mass production, making it accessible to small and medium manufacturers.
• Flexibility to switch between furniture designs between batches; allows the manufacturer to offer a range of styles and update designs in response to changing consumer preferences.
• Batch production is well suited to seasonal demand for garden furniture; stock can be built up in winter and sold in spring/summer without maintaining year-round continuous production.
• Sand casting, typical of batch production for cast iron, can produce complex decorative forms (scroll work, botanical motifs) that reflect the aesthetic value of traditional cast iron furniture.
Disadvantages of batch production compared to mass production:
• Higher unit cost than mass production because tooling investment is spread over a smaller number of units, and manual processes require more labour per item.
• Longer setup time between batches as moulds are prepared and tooling changed; this reduces overall production efficiency.
• Greater variability in component quality compared to highly automated mass production; sand casting requires more post-casting finishing (grinding, shot blasting).
• Mass production would produce each item far more quickly and at lower unit cost if demand justified it, with tighter dimensional consistency.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion of at least two developed advantages and two disadvantages of batch vs mass production, linked to cast iron furniture context (tooling cost, flexibility, quality, unit cost). Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; poor balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial.]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following fibres comes from the cocoon of the silkworm?
A) Cashmere
B) Mohair
C) Silk
D) Angora
practice_questions.marks: C) Silk [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two properties of cotton that make it suitable for everyday clothing.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: soft and comfortable against skin [1]; high absorbency (draws moisture away from the body) [1]; easy to dye in a wide range of colours [1]; breathable [1]; easy to wash [1]. (1 mark each; max 2.)

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a blended fibre and give one example of a common blend, explaining why the two fibres are combined.
practice_questions.marks: A blended fibre combines two or more different fibre types in the same yarn [1]. Example: cotton/polyester blend [1]. The combination gives cotton’s softness and breathability together with polyester’s strength, wrinkle resistance and durability [1]. (Accept other valid examples with explanation.)

practice_questions.text: Explain why elastane is never used alone as a fabric but is always used in a blend with other fibres.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks from:
• Pure elastane fabric does not hold its shape when not under tension [1] because the fibre has no recovery mechanism to maintain a fixed form when unloaded [1]
• Elastane is blended at low percentages (typically 2–20%) [1] to add stretch and recovery to a fabric structure that would otherwise be dimensionally stable [1]
• Without a structural fibre (e.g. polyester or nylon) the fabric would not provide the support and coverage needed in garments such as swimwear or sportswear [1]
(2 marks per developed point; max 4)

practice_questions.text: A designer is selecting a fibre for outdoor winter activewear. Compare wool and polyester as candidate fibres for this application, considering insulation, moisture management and sustainability.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 5 marks for genuine comparison across the three criteria:
• Insulation: wool has naturally high insulating properties from its crimped fibre structure trapping air; polyester fleece also insulates well but does not regulate temperature as naturally [1 comparison point]
• Moisture management: wool absorbs up to 30% of its weight in moisture vapour before feeling wet, keeping the wearer comfortable; polyester has low moisture absorption but wicks moisture away from the skin via capillary action in engineered weave structures [1 comparison point]
• Sustainability: wool is a renewable natural fibre from grazing animals; polyester is derived from petrochemicals; however, wool requires significant land and water for sheep farming [1 comparison point]
• Award additional marks for developed analysis (up to 2 more): e.g. wool is naturally fire-resistant and biodegradable; polyester is easier to care for (machine washable, quick-drying) [max 5 total]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using synthetic fibres rather than natural fibres in mass-market sports clothing. Consider performance, cost and environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed points on both sides. Advantages of synthetics: engineered performance properties (moisture-wicking, high strength, low weight); consistent quality and no seasonal variation in supply; lower cost in mass production; easier to add functional finishes (water-repellent coatings, antimicrobial treatments). Disadvantages: petrochemical origin; microplastics shed in washing and enter waterways; lower biodegradability at end of life; some synthetics retain body odour more than natural fibres. Reaches a reasoned judgement acknowledging that the optimal outcome may be performance blends with sustainability improvements (e.g. recycled polyester from PET bottles).
Secure: Two or more developed points on each side; judgement present.
Developing: Points on both sides but limited development.
Emerging: Mainly one side or superficial.

practice_questions.text:
Approximately how many times can paper fibre be recycled before it becomes too short to use further?
A) 1-2 times
B) 3-4 times
C) 5-7 times
D) 10-12 times
practice_questions.marks: C) 5-7 times [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two of the 6 Rs that are most directly applicable to reducing the environmental impact of a single-use food carton.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: Rethink / Refuse / Reduce / Recycle / Reuse. Answer must include a brief indication that the student understands which R is being named and why it applies. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a designer could apply the principle of Reduce when specifying a board for a supermarket cereal box.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
- The designer could specify a lower board gauge (e.g. 300 g/m2 rather than 350 g/m2) to use less material per carton while still meeting structural requirements.
- Optimising the net shape and arrangement on the sheet (imposition) to minimise offcut waste reduces the total board consumed per unit produced.
- Designing a more compact box that holds the same volume of product with less surface area reduces the total board required per carton. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why FSC certification is important to a designer specifying virgin-fibre board for a product brief.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- FSC certification guarantees that the timber used to make the board was harvested from forests managed to strict environmental standards, where replanting matches or exceeds felling rates.
- This ensures the designer can demonstrate responsible material sourcing to a client who has a sustainability policy or who markets their products on environmental credentials.
- The FSC logo on the finished product provides verifiable evidence of responsible sourcing that consumers and retailers can trust, unlike unverified environmental claims.
- Using FSC-certified board helps maintain long-term forest cover and biodiversity, sequestering carbon and protecting habitats rather than contributing to deforestation. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Using a point-of-sale food packaging display as a context, explain how two different board materials and two different finishing processes could be combined to meet functional, aesthetic and sustainability requirements.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Corrugated double-wall board for the structural base and sides of the display unit provides the compressive strength needed to bear product weight without adding excessive weight to the unit itself.
- Duplex board for the printed graphics panels provides a white, coated printing surface for high-quality brand imagery, at a lower cost and with recycled-content backing compared with solid white board.
- Gloss lamination on the graphics panels protects the print from grease, moisture and handling damage in a busy retail environment, extending the functional life of the display.
- UV spot varnish on the logo and hero product image increases shelf visibility and communicates premium brand values at point of sale.
- Both board types are recyclable at end of life: the display can be broken down into the retailer's cardboard stream, meeting sustainability requirements for a retail client.
[6 marks - Mastering: Two materials and two finishes clearly justified against functional, aesthetic and sustainability requirements with reference to the POS display context. Secure: Two materials or finishes identified with some justification but coverage of all three requirement types incomplete. Developing: One material and one finish described; limited justification. Emerging: Vague material or finish identified with no justification.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of paper and board as packaging materials compared with rigid plastics, considering sustainability, function and consumer perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of paper and board:
- Paper and board are biodegradable and break down within months in compost or soil, unlike rigid plastics which persist for hundreds of years.
- Paper fibre is recyclable up to five to seven times and is collected and processed through a well-established, near-universal UK kerbside recycling infrastructure, giving high actual recycling rates (above 70% for packaging board).
- Paper and board are made from a renewable resource (managed forestry) certified by bodies such as the FSC, unlike petroleum-based plastics which depend on a finite fossil fuel supply.
- Consumer perception of paper-based packaging is strongly positive; research consistently shows that shoppers associate cardboard packaging with environmental responsibility, which supports brand values in environmentally aware markets.
Disadvantages of paper and board:
- Paper and board provide little barrier to moisture and oxygen without additional coatings or laminates, limiting their use in packaging wet, fatty or oxygen-sensitive products compared with plastics that provide an inherent barrier.
- Rigid plastic packaging is generally lighter per unit volume than board, reducing transport emissions per product; it also offers superior impact protection for fragile goods.
- Multi-material paper and board constructions (foil-lined cartons, laminated board) are difficult to recycle and in practice are often sent to landfill or energy recovery, undermining the recyclability advantage.
- Paper and board packaging typically has a shorter functional life before it loses structural integrity under moisture or handling, whereas rigid plastic containers can be reused many times.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion across sustainability, functional performance and consumer perception with at least two developed points on each side. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages identified with some development across at least two of the three dimensions. Developing: Points listed with limited development; coverage of only one dimension. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of the matrix in a composite material?
A) It provides high tensile strength and stiffness
B) It binds the reinforcement, distributes loads and protects it from damage
C) It adds UV resistance to the composite
D) It replaces the need for reinforcement fibres in load-bearing applications
practice_questions.marks: B) It binds the reinforcement, distributes loads and protects it from damage [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the reinforcement material and the matrix material used in GRP.
practice_questions.marks:
• Reinforcement: glass fibre [1 mark]
• Matrix: polyester resin OR epoxy resin [1 mark]
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two properties of Kevlar that make it suitable for use in body armour.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks (1 per property, plus 1 for development of one):
• Very high tensile strength — roughly five times stronger than steel by weight — meaning a bullet cannot easily pass through the fibres (1).
• High toughness / impact resistance — it absorbs energy by deforming rather than shattering, spreading the impact across a larger area of the vest (1).
• Lightweight — being lighter than equivalent steel protection, it allows the wearer to move freely (1).
[Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why CFRP is used by Airbus in aircraft structures rather than steel. Refer to specific material properties in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per developed point:
• CFRP has a much higher strength-to-weight ratio than steel (1), meaning structural components can be made lighter, reducing the overall aircraft weight and therefore fuel burn per passenger (1).
• CFRP is resistant to corrosion unlike steel (1), which reduces maintenance requirements and avoids the mass of protective coatings needed on steel structures (1).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the suitability of CFRP and GRP for the hull of a racing yacht. Consider cost, weight, strength and manufacturing in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for developed comparative points (not just listing one material's properties):
• CFRP is significantly lighter than GRP for the same structural strength (1), which is critical for a racing yacht where speed depends on minimising displacement (1).
• GRP is considerably cheaper to produce than CFRP because glass fibre costs less than carbon fibre and the resin can be applied by hand lay-up without autoclave curing (1).
• CFRP is more difficult to repair after impact damage (it shatters rather than deforming); GRP can be patched more easily with additional resin and mat (1).
• For a racing yacht where performance is paramount and budget allows, CFRP is the justified choice; GRP suits leisure boats where cost is more important than optimum weight (1).
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using wearable electronic textiles in professional sports clothing compared with conventional sportswear.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of advantages (real-time biometric monitoring — heart rate, motion, temperature; personalised training data; no need to wear separate devices; potential injury prevention) and disadvantages (durability under washing and stretching, higher cost, data privacy concerns, battery life, laundry and care complications). Judgement about the balance of benefits and barriers for professional versus consumer use.
Secure: Two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with some technical context (e.g. conductive yarns, encapsulation, washing limitations); conclusion present.
Developing: Points mostly listed; limited development; one side stronger.
Emerging: Simple advantages and disadvantages with minimal explanation; no judgement.
[8 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text:
Which production scale involves making a set quantity of identical items before reconfiguring the production line for a different product?
A) One-off production
B) Batch production
C) Mass production
D) Just-in-time production
practice_questions.marks: B) Batch production [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two of the 6Rs and give one example of how each can be applied to reduce textile waste.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per correct R + relevant textile example. Accept any two of: Reduce — efficient zero-waste pattern cutting; Reuse — second-hand clothing market; Recycle — rPET from plastic bottles; Rethink — circular fashion take-back schemes; Refuse — not buying PFAS-treated fabrics; Repair — mending torn garments instead of discarding. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe three features of fast fashion that make it environmentally damaging.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Large numbers of trend-led garments are produced very quickly and sold at low prices, encouraging consumers to buy frequently and discard rapidly, leading to enormous landfill volumes.
• Fast fashion relies heavily on synthetic fibres (polyester, nylon) which shed microplastics in the wash and take hundreds of years to degrade.
• Production is often concentrated in countries with lower environmental regulation, leading to significant water pollution from textile dyeing and finishing chemical discharge. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the advantages and one limitation of using recycled polyester (rPET) instead of virgin polyester in a range of outdoor fleece jackets.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• rPET is made from post-consumer plastic bottles or textile waste, so it reduces dependence on crude oil — a finite non-renewable resource.
• Producing rPET uses approximately 59% less energy than virgin polyester, reducing the carbon footprint of the jacket.
• Using rPET allows the brand to communicate a credible sustainability claim to environmentally conscious consumers, supporting marketing and brand image.
• Limitation: rPET fleece still sheds microplastic fibres during washing, entering waterways and the food chain — the primary environmental harm of synthetic fleece is not eliminated by switching to rPET.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a fashion brand could apply the principles of circular fashion to a range of children's school uniform, and evaluate the challenges the brand would face.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Circular fashion for school uniform could involve a take-back scheme: parents return outgrown garments to the school or brand in exchange for a discount, and garments in good condition are resold as second-hand uniform, extending product life.
• Garments could be designed for durability and repairability — robust seams, replaceable logos, reinforced knees — so they last long enough to be worn by multiple children.
• Chemical recycling of end-of-life garments could return fibres to reusable raw material; however, most school shirts are polycotton blends, which are difficult to separate for recycling because the cotton and polyester fibres are intimately mixed.
• Challenge: take-back schemes require logistics infrastructure (collection, sorting, quality checking) that adds cost — and school uniform margins are already low, so the economics are difficult without a price premium or government incentive.
• Challenge: parents and schools may be sceptical of second-hand uniform or may not engage with return schemes, limiting collection volumes.
[6 marks — Mastering: Two circular strategies explained with specific application to uniform, challenges evaluated with specific obstacles identified. Secure: Two strategies with some challenge discussion. Developing: One strategy explained; challenge mentioned but not evaluated. Emerging: Vague or only sustainability listed without circular model.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages for a clothing manufacturer of switching from conventional cotton to organic cotton as the primary fibre for its range of basic T-shirts.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of organic cotton:
• Grown without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers, reducing harm to soil microbiomes, local water systems and the health of farm workers — a significant ethical and environmental improvement over conventional cotton, which uses 6% of the world's pesticides despite covering only 2.4% of farmland.
• Organic certification (e.g. GOTS) provides a credible marketing claim that can justify a premium retail price and attract sustainability-conscious consumers, potentially improving margin.
• Using organic cotton reduces the manufacturer's exposure to future chemical regulation risk as governments tighten restrictions on pesticide use in supply chains.
Disadvantages of organic cotton:
• Organic cotton yields approximately 25% less per hectare than conventional cotton, meaning more land is needed to grow the same fibre volume — a land-use trade-off that may have negative biodiversity impacts if natural habitat is converted to farmland.
• Organic cotton costs significantly more to buy than conventional cotton, increasing raw material cost and either compressing margins or raising retail prices — a problem for a basic T-shirt competing primarily on price.
• The water consumption of organic cotton production is broadly similar to conventional; transitioning to organic does not address cotton's fundamental water intensity problem.
• Supply of certified organic cotton is limited relative to global demand; scaling up production would require years of transition for conventional farms, creating supply chain risk.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion with at least two developed points per side and specific data/evidence; limitations acknowledged for both the advantages and disadvantages. Secure: Two points per side with development. Developing: Points listed, some imbalance or limited development. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial.]

practice_questions.text:
Which scale of production is most appropriate for manufacturing 50,000 identical flat-pack bookcase panels per week?
A) One-off production
B) Batch production
C) Mass production
D) Jobbing production
practice_questions.marks: C) Mass production [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two strategies from the 6 Rs framework that specifically reduce the environmental impact of timber sourcing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: Refuse (declining uncertified timber sources) / Reuse (specifying reclaimed timber) / Reduce (CNC nesting to minimise off-cuts) / Recycle (manufactured boards from sawmill waste) / Repair (designing for maintenance and longevity). Accept any two distinct strategies with a brief description. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how CNC nesting software reduces material waste in the mass production of flat-pack furniture panels.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• CNC nesting software arranges all the required panel shapes digitally on a virtual representation of the manufactured board sheet before cutting begins.
• The software calculates the most efficient arrangement to minimise the area of board left as off-cuts, reducing material waste per sheet.
• The cutting paths are sent directly to the CNC router, which cuts all panels in sequence without the operator needing to re-mark or re-measure, maintaining accuracy and consistency. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why cross-laminated timber (CLT) is considered a lower-carbon alternative to reinforced concrete for the structure of a new school building.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Trees absorb CO2 during their growth; the carbon is locked into the CLT panels for the lifetime of the building rather than being released, so CLT acts as a carbon store rather than a carbon source.
• Producing reinforced concrete requires burning limestone (calcination) and smelting steel for reinforcement, both of which release large quantities of CO2; CLT production requires only drying and bonding timber with adhesive, a far less energy-intensive process.
• CLT panels can be prefabricated off-site to precise dimensions and erected quickly, reducing the energy used on site during construction.
• At the end of the building's life, CLT panels can potentially be reused or chipped for biomass energy; demolished concrete has very limited recycling options.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the 6 Rs framework can be applied throughout the design, production and disposal of a timber garden bench. Use specific strategies in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Refuse: specify only FSC-certified hardwood such as oak or teak from certified plantations, refusing to use uncertified tropical timber that may have come from illegally logged rainforest.
• Reduce: use CNC nesting to minimise off-cuts from sawn boards; use finger joints to use shorter off-cut lengths that would otherwise be wasted.
• Reuse: use reclaimed railway sleepers or reclaimed oak, which are already seasoned and require no new felling.
• Recycle: at end of life, untreated timber components can be chipped for garden mulch or biomass fuel; metal fixings can be separated and sent for metal recycling.
• Repair: use screwed joints (rather than adhesive-only) so a cracked rail can be removed and replaced; specify a penetrating oil finish that can be re-applied without full surface stripping.
• Rethink: consider whether a thermally modified timber (which needs no chemical preservative) would deliver the same rot resistance as pressure-treated pine, avoiding chemical treatment waste.
[6 marks — Mastering: At least three distinct Rs applied with specific named strategies and product context. Secure: Two or three Rs applied with some development. Developing: One R or vague references. Emerging: Superficial mention of recycling only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using mass production with manufactured boards for a range of flat-pack bedroom furniture, compared with batch production using solid timber.
practice_questions.marks:
Mass production with manufactured boards advantages:
• Very low unit cost because high automation (CNC cutting, edge-banding, KD-fitting insertion) minimises labour per unit; flat-pack packaging further reduces transport and storage costs.
• Manufactured boards such as chipboard are dimensionally stable and will not warp or split over time, giving consistent quality without the variability of solid timber.
• Large sheet sizes allow components to be efficiently nested with minimal waste, and the boards use low-grade timber fibres and sawmill by-products (Reduce/Recycle).
• Products are standardised for mass-market consumers who prioritise affordability and availability over craftsmanship.
Mass production disadvantages:
• Formaldehyde binders in chipboard and MDF off-gas VOCs, which is a concern in enclosed bedrooms; premium products require CARB2-compliant low-emission boards.
• Flat-pack furniture is difficult to repair if damaged; cam-lock fittings weaken after repeated assembly and disassembly, and chipboard edges crumble, making the product less durable than solid timber.
• The standardised appearance of mass-produced furniture offers no aesthetic differentiation; consumers seeking uniqueness or quality craftsmanship will not value it.
Batch production with solid timber advantages:
• Products can be customised to client specifications (dimensions, finish, species) in a way that mass production cannot accommodate.
• Solid timber furniture can be repaired, refinished and will last decades, reducing lifetime environmental impact despite the higher initial cost.
Batch production disadvantages:
• Higher unit cost due to skilled labour; setting up jigs and templates for each batch adds time and cost not present in continuous mass production.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages per approach, applied to bedroom furniture context. Secure: Two of each with some development. Developing: Limited development or imbalanced. Emerging: Superficial or one-sided.]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a twill weave?
A) Weft passes over one warp thread and under the next in every row
B) Warp threads float over four or more weft threads before interlacing
C) Weft passes over two or more warp threads before going under one, creating a diagonal rib
D) Fibres are bonded together without spinning or weaving
practice_questions.marks: C) Weft passes over two or more warp threads before going under one, creating a diagonal rib [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one reason why felt does not fray when cut.
practice_questions.marks: Felt has no woven or knitted structure [1 mark] / fibres are bonded together by heat, moisture and pressure rather than interlaced, so there are no free yarn ends to unravel [1 mark]. (Either reason accepted for 1 mark.)

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between warp knit and weft knit fabric in terms of yarn direction and the risk of laddering.
practice_questions.marks: Weft knit: yarn runs horizontally across the fabric; stitches interlock with those above and below [1]; susceptible to laddering if a stitch breaks because the column can unravel downward [1]. Warp knit: multiple yarns run vertically (lengthways) simultaneously [1]; does not ladder because each yarn is linked laterally to adjacent yarns, preventing column unravelling [1]. (Award up to 3 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Explain why satin weave is used for evening dress linings rather than plain weave.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks from:
• Satin weave has long warp floats over four or more weft threads [1] which lie flat on the surface to give a smooth, lustrous appearance appropriate for eveningwear [1]
• Satin weave has very few interlacement points [1] which allows the fabric to drape fluidly against the body [1]
• Plain weave has the maximum number of interlacement points, making it stiff and low-draping [1] which would not hang smoothly inside an evening dress [1]
(2 marks per developed comparison point; max 4)

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating a high-performance sports top for long-distance running. Explain, with reference to fabric construction and fibre choice, what properties the fabric must have and justify a suitable combination. Include one disadvantage of your chosen construction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies relevant performance requirements for the product (moisture management, stretch for movement, lightweight, durability). Recommends a specific construction (e.g. weft knit for stretch) with a specific fibre or blend (e.g. polyester for moisture-wicking / low absorption, with elastane for stretch recovery). Justifies how the construction and fibre together achieve the required properties. Identifies a genuine disadvantage (e.g. weft knit susceptible to laddering; polyester sheds microplastics in washing).
Secure: Identifies 2+ relevant properties, recommends a named construction and fibre with some justification, identifies one disadvantage.
Developing: Recommends a construction but justification is limited or fibre choice is vague.
Emerging: Lists properties without linking to a construction or fibre.

practice_questions.text: Compare the suitability of plain weave and weft knit fabric for producing a reusable shopping bag. Consider strength, stretch, ease of manufacture and sustainability.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 5 marks for genuine comparative analysis across criteria:
• Strength: plain weave has high interlacement density giving greater tensile and tear resistance than weft knit, which is important for a bag carrying heavy loads [1 comparison]
• Stretch: weft knit has high stretch; for a bag this may cause the bag to deform under load and not recover its shape; plain weave is dimensionally stable under load [1 comparison]
• Ease of manufacture: both can be produced industrially at scale; plain weave bags (e.g. cotton tote) are cut and sewn; weft knit would require shaping or cutting that may encourage fraying without a selvedge [1 comparison]
• Sustainability: cotton plain weave can be biodegradable at end of life; a synthetic weft knit (polyester) is not biodegradable but may have lower production carbon footprint [1 comparison]
• Additional developed analysis up to 5 marks total.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an advantage of using CAM in manufacturing?
A) It eliminates the need for skilled designers
B) It produces identical parts consistently without operator fatigue
C) It reduces the initial capital cost of machinery
D) It can produce parts without any input from CAD software
practice_questions.marks: B) It produces identical parts consistently without operator fatigue [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two disadvantages of using CAD software in a small design business.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per disadvantage (any two):
• High software licence cost
• Significant training time required before productivity improves
• Requires powerful and expensive hardware
• Digital files can be copied, creating intellectual property risks
• Loss of server access or cyberattack can destroy design data
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a laser cutter would be used to produce an acrylic panel for a product prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• The acrylic sheet is placed flat on the laser cutter bed (1).
• A vector file (from CAD software) is loaded and the machine is set to the correct power and speed for the material thickness (1).
• The laser beam cuts along the defined paths, producing the panel shape with a very narrow kerf and smooth edges that may require no further finishing (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer would choose 3D printing (FDM) rather than CNC routing to produce a one-off prototype of a hollow enclosure for an electronic device.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per developed point:
• 3D printing can produce hollow internal geometries directly, whereas CNC routing is limited to surface features and cannot easily create enclosed internal cavities in a single operation (1). This means the enclosure can be built as one piece with a lid and internal ribbing all included in a single print (1).
• 3D printing requires no tooling or fixturing specific to the shape — only the digital file is needed (1). For a one-off prototype, this eliminates the set-up cost and time that a CNC routing operation would require (1).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school workshop has a budget to purchase one machine for making acrylic and MDF components for GCSE D&T projects. Compare the suitability of a laser cutter and a CNC router for this purpose.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for comparative points:
• A laser cutter can cut acrylic and MDF cleanly with a very narrow kerf and no cutting forces, reducing the risk of workpiece distortion or material fracture in thin sheet work (1).
• A CNC router can cut thicker MDF and solid wood that a laser cutter cannot safely process; it is also capable of 3D relief carving, extending what students can make (1).
• A laser cutter can engrave text and patterns onto flat sheet surfaces rapidly, which is useful for design decoration (1).
• Both require CAD files and safety enclosures; the laser cutter requires ventilation for fumes from acrylic and MDF cutting (1).
• For a GCSE workshop focused on flat sheet work, the laser cutter’s precision, minimal kerf and ability to engrave may make it the more versatile choice; for a workshop producing structural 3D woodwork, the CNC router offers greater depth capacity (1).
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using CNC manufacturing rather than manual craft production for a batch of 500 identical timber jewellery boxes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of CNC advantages (consistency, 24-hour operation, complex joint geometry, reduced operator error, optimised nesting minimises material waste) and disadvantages (high capital cost of machinery, significant set-up and programming time, maintenance requires specialist engineers, single point of failure if machine breaks down, loss of craftsperson skills). Weighted judgement about whether CNC is justified at a batch of 500.
Secure: Two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with specific context (e.g. nesting, kerf, batch size economics); conclusion present.
Developing: Points mostly listed; limited development; one side stronger.
Emerging: Simple pros/cons; no specific context or judgement.
[8 marks — levels-based]
